There are approximately 1,400, but I am advised several hundred have not yet

Soldiers' Pensions
been received. Then, thirdly, I am to state the material allegations contained therein. Those can be briefly stated as follows: In February, 1932, the Dominion government changed certain regulations under the Old Age Pensions Act. One of those changed regulations has enabled the provincial board in British Columbia, who administer old age pensions in that province, to claim that they have the right to refuse a pension to anyone who, under the provisions of the Parents Maintenance Act of British Columbia, has not sued his children. The petitioners claim that such a condition is undesirable for three reasons: First, it is unnatural ; secondly, it is utterly useless, because often the children are not able even to support themselves and, thirdly, there is no money [DOT]with which old age pension applicants can sue their children.
Then, the prayer of the petition is as follows:
Therefore your petitioners respectfully urge that the said amendment shall be repealed immediately.
In justice to these people I should add that the petition is an entirely spontaneous expression of their own. I had nothing to do with the instigation of it, although I heartily agree with it.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask
the Minister of Finance if he has any announcement to make in regard to the provision in the budget address dealing with pensions?

speakeroldname: Hon. E. N. RHODES (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rose at the same time as the hon. member for the purpose of making the announcement to which he has referred. With respect to the announcement contained in the budget regarding pensioners, who are in the employ of the government, it will be recalled that on March 24, last I made a statement which reads, in part, as follows:
Perhaps in this connection, however, I might be permitted to say one word, as there would appear to be some considerable misapprehension with regard to what is in the mind of the government in respect to pensions. The last thing in the world that we had in mind was any interference with the sanctity of the contract concerning pensions. Whatever merit there may or may not be attached to the suggestions contained in the budget speech with respect to pensions, it was never intended to interfere with pensions as such.
This will be found at page 3354 of Hansard. I may add further that it was never at any time contemplated that there should be any discrimination shown towards the returned soldier, especially as contrasted with what may be termed the civilian employee. On the contrary the whole proposal emanated from a desire to afford, during this period of distress, an opportunity to the returned soldier who served his country faithfully, but who, at the moment, finds himself, through no fault of his own, without either pension or employment, as contrasted with some of his comrades who, at the moment, receive a pension, and at the same time are given employment with the full salary attached to the position. To this course objection has been taken by representatives of the several returned soldier organizations upon two main grounds: First, that it would in effect, result in a violation of agreement or contract; and, secondly, would be taken as an example by other employers with detrimental results.
The whole position has been the subject of careful review at two conferences, the first held on March 24, and the second on April 19. At these conferences, the following were present, representing their respective organizations:
Major John S. Roper, M.C., K.C., President, Canadian Legion, British Empire Service League; Mr. J. R. Bowler, Canadian Legion, British Empire Service League; Mr. Richard Hale, representing Tuberculous Reference Section, Canadian Legion; Colonel W. C. H. Wood, Captain C. P. Gilman, Doctor P. B. Mellon, representing Army and Navy Veterans in Canada; Mr. Frank G. J. McDonagh,
Private Bills

representing Canadian Pensioners' Association of the Great War; Captain (Reverend) Sydney E. Lambert, Dominion President of the Amputations Association of the Great War; Captain E. A. Baker, M.C., representing the Sir Arthur Pearson Club of Blinded Soldiers and Sailors; Mr. Richard Myers, representing Amputations Association of the Great War.
After full discussion it was agreed that there would, for the present, be no interference with the existing procedure, but it was agreed:
1.	That any consideration of a general readjustment of the rate of pensions should be postponed until the next session of parliament.
2.	That an amendment shall be made to the Income War Tax Act providing that pensions shall be subject to income tax.
3.	That on and after May 1, 1933, there are to be no additions of dependents to the list of those who are eligible, or who may become eligible for pensions.
I desire further to announce that, as a result of extreme care in reviewing existing pensions, it is believed that while affording full protection to those who are justly entitled to pension, certain irregularities which have arisen through misrepresentation, whether fraudulent or otherwise, on the part of certain applicants will be remedied, and that this course will effect a substantial saving for the treasury.
In conclusion may I express on behalf of the government our appreciation for the generous cooperation we have received from the representatives of the above-named service organizations, and for the fair and reasonable manner in which they carried on their discussions and made their representations on behalf of the members of their several organizations.

The treaty of February 24, 1925, made the international boundary commissioners responsible for the permanent maintenance in a state of effective demarcation of the entire international boundary between Canada and the United States and between Canada and Alaska, including that section of the boundary through the St. Lawrence river and great lakes.
Since 1925 the commission has made surveys necessary for locating and marking the boundary at a number of points on the St. Lawrence, Niagara, Detroit and St. Clair rivers. Necessary repairs to a number of reference monuments and the erection and location of others to replace several monuments washed out or otherwise destroyed are to be undertaken in the near future.
That gives a brief resume of the work of the international boundary commission. We are under obligation by these treaties to keep up our work comparably with that carried on by the United States. We are now slightly behind in our program and the extra amount asked for is to enable us to bring our work up to their level.

May I ask the minister to consider the necessity of marking a boundary between the United States and Canada in the district I have the honour to represent, namely, in the Semiahmoo bay, which is about ten and a half or eleven miles wide. There is no distinguishing mark across the whole length of the bay, with the result that difficulties, have arisen in the past in connection with fishing rights. The American fishing concerns have placed traps so close to the Canadian boundary that there have been doubts as to whether they were in Canadian or American waters. I appealed to the Minister of Fisheries and he was good enough to say that he was in favour of some distinguishing mark being placed there. I plead now with the Minister of the Interior. There has never been a mark in that bay and it is impossible to tell, standing on the shore, whether a fish trap is in Canadian or in American waters. Will the minister take the matter under advisement with a view to having a mark placed?

I beg the hon. member's

It seems to me that this is

Advancement of forest conservation; national inventory of forest resources; investigation of forest conditions and rates of growth-[DOT]
And so on, amounting to $266,000. What work was done in connection with advancement of forest conservation?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
This item is to cover the contribution by the dominion for the advancement of forestry in Canada. At the present time we have three laboratories, one situated at Vancouver, carrying on experimental work
Supply-Interior-Forestry

with British Columbia woods, one located in Montreal where the possibilities of the pulp and paper industry are being scientifically investigated, and our general laboratory at Ottawa where work of a more general nature is undertaken. Valuable assistance is also given in preparing information that will assist the industry in marketing Canadian forest products. In addition to that the Forestry branch, in cooperation with the various provinces, is endeavouring to make an inventory of the forest resources of the dominion. The information is supplied to the greater extent by the provinces and is compiled by the department at Ottawa. Besides that, scientific investigations are carried on by the department in the field as to the rates of growth of timber, forest protection, fire hazard research, timber land management, the study of wood lots on farms for the assistance of the farming community generally, and various other scientific studies. That, briefly, constitutes the duties and responsibilities of the Forestry branch of the department at the present time.

Is the Forestry branch still
operating the forestry farm at Indian Head and are any trees being distributed by the department?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Those stations were transferred two years ago to the Department of Agriculture, but the work is being carried on, I understand, by that department and trees distributed throughout the three prairie provinces by the stations at Indian Head and Sutherland.

I assume the work in

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs

We have in the various
provinces our own officers who are working in cooperation with the provincial forestry departments in laying down certain standard methods of procedure. As the information is supplied almost entirely by officials of the provincial governments, our branch compiles the figures as they are submitted to them by the provinces. In some cases assistance is given by the various large companies who may have holdings in the different provinces.

any great length of time and therefore I anticipate it will be some years yet before it is completed.

Would the minister give us the names of the branches which have been taken away from the Department of the Interior since the present administration took office, and whether it is contemplated to take away any more from that department?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There have been certain amalgamations within the department, but no branch has been done away with. Certain portions of different branches have been given to other departments. A moment ago I instanced the nursery stations at Indian Head and Sutherland, which were transferred to the Department of Agriculture. Formerly they were under the control of the Forestry branch of the Department of the Interior. No branches, as such, have been taken over by other departments.
Have they been taken over by the provinces?

speechtext: No.

The expenditures in the department have been reduced to one-third of what they were previously. How is that reduction explained? Surely there must have been a great deal of work taken away from the department?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: On account of the transfer of natural resources to the three prairie provinces, a great deal of work was eliminated. Those provinces are now doing part of the work which was formerly done by the Department of the Interior. However the branches which formerly administered the natural resources are carrying on with a much reduced program.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There were 1,087 retired as a result of the transfer of resources.
Have any of those been taken back into the service, and any compensation given to them-retiring allowance, or anything of that nature?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
All those who were retired received retiring allowance or superannuation, as the case might be. Those employees who were retired from the Department of the Interior, owing to transfer of resources, have
been and are being absorbed into the service of various other branches of the government. In fact there is an order in council in existence which directs the Civil Service Commission to follow that procedure in cases where the employees have the qualifications necessary to fill the vacancies as they occur.
Will the minister say how many are still out, or how many have been taken back?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes. Of the number retired, 137 are now employed temporarily in other branches. In addition to that 256 permanent employees and 22 temporary employees have been taken over by the three provinces.
There are about 500 still out of employment?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Some of the employees are not anxious to be reemployed in the service-They prefer to take their superannuations; and retire permanently. The others are being: absorbed in the other departments as rapidly as conditions permit.

Is it contemplated to transfer any branches of the department to other departments, as has been done in the past? There was a time when the Department of the Interior covered the whole of the problems in the western country, but as time went on control over immigration, mines and other activities was transferred. I should like to know whether there is still any need for the existence of a Department of the Interior, and whether any heed is going to be taken to the requests, made by business men in different sections of Canada, concerning the curtailment of the number of departments? Can the minister tell us whether there is any movement in that direction?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Not to my knowledge,
Mr. Chairman.

I should
like to bring to the attention of the minister a few things that have been on my mind in connection with national parks. I should like to see the minister complete that agreement with the British Columbia government for the inclusion of Mount Robson park. I think that while the government of British Columbia are in a mood to do so that agreement should be proceeded with and completed.
The other matter is this. While I would be the last one to complain about expenditure on the new highway from Jasper to Lake Louise, nevertheless I think that for the sake of having a trans-Canada highway through
Supply-Interior-Forestry

tihe mountains to the coast it would have been well to continue the expenditure on that project even to the extent of helping the British Columbia government. But more particularly would I stress the point that, having obtained the area known as Mount Robson park, the money should be expended to build a highway from Jasper westward to connect with the highway that will be constructed around the Columbia river. I am not raising any objection to the expenditure on the highway across the summit, but at the same time it hardly seems wise to build a highway across the summit and let remain in abeyance the completion of a highway via Edmonton and Jasper connecting with the southern highway that will connect Vancouver with Calgary, Banff and Lake Louise. I merely plead for the prosecution of those highways which will serve all the public. It will be very nice of course to go to Jasper and down across ithe new 'highway to Banff, but what I am asking for is the construction of the main highway to give us access to the coast, or indeed to take the circular trip if that is desirable via the new Columbia river highway, back by Golden and Lake Louise and Banff. I rather regret that the project across the summit seems to be getting the preference in construction. I would much prefer to see the other under construction, so that the citizens of northern Saskatchewan and northern Alberta will have a direct highway to the coast as well as the citizens of the southern end of those provinces.
In considering a program for this year I would plead with the minister that those projects be concluded before you attempt to complete the highway over the summit because it will be a somewhat expensive undertaking and in my opinion it will not serve such a large number of patrons as if the construction were made by the route I have suggested.

There is a small amount
included in this total that I am a little curious about. That is an amount of $1,500 to provide for expropriation of areas for right of way on the Savona-Port Moody section of the main line of the Canadian Pacific railway, also on the Pembina and Stonewall branches of the same road. Why is the Dominion government called upon to provide money to expropriate areas on the right of way of the Canadian Pacific railway?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
In connection with those portions of the Canadian Pacific Railway which were constructed by the Dominion government and afterwards turned over to the
 |! 2
railway company, it is provided in the contract between the dominion and- the company that the necessary right of way for the railway will be acquired by the government where necessary. Before this department had advice as to what lands were affected by the right of way a certain number of patents were issued which contained no reservation of the lands required for the railway. Many years ago the necessary deeds were obtained from owners in a large number of cases, but some cases have remained unsettled up to the present time. The areas in each case are small, but in addition to paying for the land the government has to provide the necessary expenses for legal work connected with the transfer of title. It is impossible to forecast what expenditure may be required, as there are no means of knowing what price will be demanded by the various owners, nor are there any means of estimating what amount will be required for legal services, and possibly for expropriation proceedings. The sum of $1,500 is named merely as affording a basis for action to clear up these pending cases as far as possible in 1933-34. The Department of Justice has advised that it is the duty of the Dominion government to procure title for the railway in all these cases.

I would like to ask the minister if he could tell us what amount of New York exchange or gold has been given to different parties in Canada, if any, to meet payments of interest on bonds coming due in New York?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have not that information before me, I can secure it for my hon. friend, except that it is not always desirable to disclose names. But I can give amounts.

Well the government prohibited the export of gold some time last year. There is a belief among many people in Canada that the government may perhaps not have given gold to individuals, but that gold has been sent to New York to the credit of

Supply-Finance-Salaries
the government and the government may have given New York exchange to persons in Canada at a certain rate. That is the reason that I am asking the question. Could the minister say what persons were given this exchange and at what rate it was sold to them?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Speaking offhand, I do not know of any instance where we have given exchange in New York. We have permitted the export of gold under licence. If it were a question of assistance as far as exchange is concerned it would be at the going rate. I do not know what particular point my hon. friend has in mind.

I think I remember seeing in the press where the government had given gold to some province at a favourable rate. From the way it was stated it looked as though it were a more favourable rate than could have been obtained at that time by buying exchange in the New York market. I just wondered whether the minister could say whether that is correct.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, Mr. Chairman, it would be the going rate in all cases as far as I am aware. I will verify that.
I would ask the minister if there is any gold going out of the country. I noticed in the paper the other day that gold was going to London, and that some banks were making money out of it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That was gold belonging to the banks. They had to receive an export licence the same as anyone else.
Could the minister tell us if that gold was in possession of the banks before the Gold Export Act was passed?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not know that I can give an accurate answer regarding that, I do not know that it is material whether it was or was not, but I would assume that it was gold that was in their possession prior to the Gold Export Act being passed.

It seems to me it makes a very material difference. No private party was allowed to export gold. Any bank that held gold that it had received prior to the passage of the Gold Export Act without paying the premium and is now allowed to export it and receive the premium certainly is getting something that the private citizen is not allowed to get. I do not see why the banks should be allowed that privilege. Anyone else having gold in their possession would have to take the legal rate for that gold. Why should the banks be allowed to export this gold and
receive a premium? Would the minister explain that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It might be to meet obligations of the banks' clients, and those clients might be municipalities, cities or provinces. That is the answer.

In that case the gold received by the banks at par is being sold by the banks at a premium, and really that seems an injustice. I do not see why they should be put in a favoured position by the action of the government, by being allowed to export gold in that way.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I can assure my hon. friend that there is no question of favouritism so far as the granting of export licences is concerned. In each instance sufficient cause for the granting of a licence must be established; exportation is only permitted upon the merits of each individual case.

Then might I ask the government whether, when the Gold Export Act was passed, containing a provision that export could be made only by the banks, it was the intention that the banks would be allowed to take advantage of that provision to export their own private holdings of gold.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Of course I cannot answer that question by saying yes or no. My hon. friend must remember that Canadian banks have branches in Cuba, in South America, in various parts of the West Indies, in Newfoundland, on the continent and in the United States. They have their obligations to meet in gold, and no doubt there are instances-in fact I have personal knowledge of some-when they must have a certain amount of gold in hand for the purpose of meeting those obligations. My hon. friend must not suggest that there is any question of favoritism because a licence is issued to a bank for the export of gold. I have known of instances when gold has been exported for the very purpose I have in mind and later brought back to this country when the necessity for the gold in the other country had passed.

There are many municipalities in Canada that have to meet obligations in the United States, and until two weeks ago they were legally entitled to get gold from this dominion. But they were told there was no use getting the gold because they could not get a licence to export it. Under those circumstances I do not see that it is right to give the banks authority to export gold which they may have held for several years. They took it in at par but now they are allowed to export it at a premium, though so far as
Supply-Finance-Salaries

I know no one else can secure that privilege. Many people have obligations to meet in the United States, but they have been refused gold and told they could not secure a licence to export it if they did obtain it. I have had people come to me who found themselves in that position; they have been told by the government that there was no use of their getting gold because they could not export it. I might refer to the case brought up the other day by the hon. member for New Westminster, who referred to a United States tourist who brought in a bank draft, some United States currency and some United States gold. The Canadian bank in Vancouver gave him a premium on the United States draft and the United States currency which he held, but they refused to give him any premium on his gold. Then, when he wanted the gold back, the bank said, "You might as well leave it with us because you cannot take it out of Canada." That tourist was a citizen of the United States, but the Gold Export Act would not allow him to take out the gold which he had brought in. Apparently under this act the banks can take gold from tourists at par and send it to the United States or England and obtain a premium on it. If that is not making favourites of the banks I do not know what you might call it. Certainly it does not seem a proper practice.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I wish to say at once, and as firmly as my vocabulary will permit, that there is no suggestion of favouritism so far as the banks are concerned. The banks are not selling gold as a merchantable commodity; they are transporting gold for the purpose of meeting obligations in foreign countries. As I said before, these obligations might be obligations of the banks, of the provinces, the cities or the municipalities. My hon. friend suggests that municipalities should be allowed to come down here and get gold without the payment of the premium. If I might say so without the slightest desire to be in the least offensive to my hon. friend, that idea seems preposterous. If we did that we would not have any gold in Canada in twenty-four hours. As a matter of fact the municipality, like anyone else, can get gold if there is excess gold so far as the government is concerned by paying the premium, and in no other way. My hon. friend does not suggest that the government should pay a premium for gold and then sell it at par.

No, I never suggested that the government should pay a premium for gold; that was the government's own idea. I have often wondered under what authority

that action was taken. Perhaps the minister would tell me by what authority the government pays a premium for gold, and whether it is the intention to continue paying that premium.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have no doubt at all that Canada will continue to pay a premium on gold. I hope it will never lose its sanity to the extent of not doing so, and until we are prepared to pass a statute confiscating gold I do not see why the practice should be discontinued. If we are going to confiscate gold, of course, we might as well contemplate the confiscation of other kinds of property. Until that time comes there is nothing to do but pay the current rate for gold.
What advantage is there to the government in paying this premium?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There is a very great advantage to the government. As a matter of fact the stimulation of the production of gold in Canada has been one of the saving factors in the present situation. It has not only enabled Canada to meet her obligations in foreign countries without undue strain and undue pressure which would be created if we attempted to buy foreign currencies with our own paper money; it has had the additional effect of stimulating the development of gold in Canada to such an extent that the Canadian gold industry to-day is the second in the world. It has given employment to many thousands of men, and my hon. friend must remember that to the extent that mining is made profitable not only do we bring about the employment of many men and provide a market for large sections of our country, but to the extent that they make money 12J per cent of that profit comes to the exchequer of Canada from the company itself. Then, when the dividends go to the individual shareholders, we get another slice of the profits by way of income tax. So, taking the balance-all round, it does seem to me that we have profited very largely by the development of the gold industry in Canada.
In that connection may I point out this fact, that to-day there are gold mines in Canada which are operated at a modest profit, and in some cases at a very bare profit, which would not be able to operate at all if they had to sell their gold without a premium. That has had a very marked effect in stimulating the development of the gold industry in Canada.

I think perhaps the minister misunderstood my last question. What I should like to know is why the government.

Supply-Finance-Insurance
does not allow the mining companies to sell their gold freely to the highest bidder. Why does the government insist that the gold be
delivered to the mint in Ottawa?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I may say to my hon.
friend that there seems to me a very important advantage to Canada in being able to secure gold at the New York price or at the London price, as the case may be, but payable in Canadian currency. If we permitted the mines to sell their gold freely and had to resort to the purchase of gold in New York or London, as the case might be, to meet our commitments we would find a strain upon our exchange which would mean a higher premium, so it is all to our advantage that we should continue the practice of having gold with which to meet our commitments.

It is difficult to understand
why we would have to pay a greater premium; we are paying whatever premium exists on New York funds at the present time, so surely there would be no difference. May I point out that although England went off the gold standard in September, 1931, the Chancellor of the Exchequer, Mr. Snowden, said it would not interfere with the free gold market, that gold would be allowed to be freely bought and sold on the London market as had been the case previously. I have been trying to find out why the government of Canada adopted this other policy of commandeering all the gold, but paying certain rates of exchange for it. I want to find out if there is any advantage to be derived from that practice.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If my hon. friend has not understood my explanation all I can say is that I am sorry. I have given an explanation which, to my mind at all events, is as clear as an explanation possibly could be. I have pointed out that there is a very distinct advantage to Canada in being able to secure gold within Canada, payable at the New York or London rate as the case may be, but payable in Canadian currency, with the gold deliverable here. If the companies shipped their gold freely to London or New York, as the case might be, and the government had to resort to the purchase of gold in New York or London to meet its obligations, exchange would stiffen and we should have to pay an appreciably higher premium in purchasing foreign currecny with our own Canadian notes. It seems to me apparent that the advantage is very markedly in favour of the present system.

The minister is trying to take advantage of two different arguments. He says that the higher the premium for gold the
better it is for the gold mines and consequently for Canada, inasmuch as it stimulates work; and now he says we should purchase gold at the exchange rate so that it will not go higher. Apparently he is now doing something which is keeping the gold mines from getting the returns which a moment ago he said they should get. He is trying to ride two horses at once.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Well, Mr. Chairman, I
give it up.

I suggest to the minister that this government has not made a very good job of handling the question of gold since September 1931. My hon. friends have until the las'; few days refused to suspend the redemption of dominion notes in gold, and they have illegally refused many requests for gold since September 1931. They have now seen the error of their ways and have passed an act which gives them power of suspension. They first suspended redemption without legal authority and then prohibited the export of gold except under licence and except by chartered banks, and now they allow the chartered banks to export gold for their own private use. So far as I know they have not allowed anyone else to do so. If they have, I should like to know who the parties are.

speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Insurance-salaries, $89,460; contingencies, $64,000.

I had no idea that the question of insurance would come up to-day, but there is one point I wish to bring to the attention of the minister, though I have not with me the necessary papers to deal with it fully. I have read that some change was made in the Insurance Act last year under which companies may allow a policy to lapse though there may be sufficient loan value in the policy to cover the premium due. It seems to me it should be a statutory condition, in any life insurance policy issued in Canada that if the policy has a stated loan value whioh is sufficient to cover a premium due the company should not be allowed to have the policy lapse because the premium is not paid. The amount necessary to cover the premium should be automatically advanced and charged as a loan against the policy. That is done under most policies which carry a clause making special provision therefor, and if that condition is not statutory it should be. I do not know whether this is under the jurisdiction of the dominion Department of Insurance, but I should like to get some information from the minister on this point. I am told that lapsed policies in the case of one com-

Supply-Finance-Insurance
pany amounted last year to S20,000,000. Many men have been unable to pay the premiums on their policies owing to the deflation to which we have been subject in the last three years, and if some of these policies carried a loan value which would cover the premium, and if the premium was not automatically advanced, then in my opinion it is a shame and the law should be changed so as to make it compulsory that in any such case the policy should be carried, the premium being automatically advanced as a loan against the policy.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Speaking offhand, I am not aware of any change in the conditions surrounding the issuing of life insurance policies as contrasted with the conditions which have hitherto obtained. I may point out however that if there was any change it was made by this parliament and is therefore a matter of the statute law of Canada, and the proper time for the hon. member to make representations will be when considering an amendment to the Insurance Act. However, I will make closer inquiry into the matter. As I say, speaking offhand, I do not think there has been any change, but if there has been it is in conformity with the Insurance Act as passed by this parliament.

An amended Insurance Act was passed last year and I protested three or four times against its being put through without previous reference to the banking and commerce committee, so that all these questions might be dealt with fully in that committee instead of in committee of the whole house. Every hon. member will recall that protests were made repeatedly against the passage of the act through the house without sending it to the committee. We asked to have it sent to the committee first. I am not sure that the act as amended last year made any change in regard to this particular point, but I am told that it did; certain sections were changed or omitted. This is a matter which in my opinion parliament cannot afford to pass without some remedial measures if the situation is as I have stated it to-day. That is the way it has been represented to me. I have been told that many policies have lapsed though they had a sufficient loan value to cover the premium due. The premium was not paid by the insured party. In many cases they took it for granted that the loan value would be used to cover the premium and that the premium would be advanced and charged automatically against the policy as a loan. The insurance policies which I carry myself contain that clause, and if there are policies issued 
without it the Insurance Act should be amended so as to make that impossible. I know that many people are under the impression that if a policy has a loan value sufficient to cover the premium, the premium will be automatically advanced. I am sorry I have not here a letter which I received recently and which would I think corroborate the statement I am making now. I should like to see the minister interest himself in this matter, and if the Insurance Act stands as I think it does it should be amended before this house rises. It would not require a long bill to do it, but the matter is too important to leave it in its present state.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will make inquiry at once.
Does the hon. member mean to say that where there was credit coming to the insured under the policy, after a request had been made for extension, the policy was cancelled?

No. The case stated to me was this, that in many instances where there was a loan value under the policy, sufficient to meet the premium, the premium was not advanced automatically the insured party not having written to the company requesting that a loan be issued and applied to the payment of the premium. I know that in many policies there is a clause which provides that if payment of the premium is not made on the due date the amount will be automatically advanced and the premium paid, and a charge will be made against the policy. My contention is that if that is not statutory it should be made so in every life insurance policy issued in Canada.

Does the
hon. gentleman suggest that it should be done without a request from the insured? I gather from what he states that the insured paid no attention to securing a loan. Is that right, or did he apply and was refused? I happen to know that a great deal of that sort of thing was done last year-not cancellations but the carrying of policies that had sufficient equity to see them through.

What I am saying is this.
Most policies contain a provision to the effect that if payment is not made by the policy holder the premium will be automatically advanced by the company itself and charged as a loan against the policy. I am not saying that in any case the company refused to make a loan to cover the premium; but where the insured does not take the trouble to write to the company to ask that that be done, it is not automatically advanced and the policy

Supply-F inance-Miscellaneous
lapses. One who tried to get his policy once again placed in good standing was told: You can have your policy put in good standing by having a medical examination. I contend that where there is a sufficient loan value on a policy to cover the premium, that premium should be automatically advanced and Charged against the policy, even though the insured does not take the trouble to write and ask that that be done. I understand a great majority of the polioies contain a clause to cover such an advance and most people take it for granted that such a clause is in their policy. However, many people do not take the trouble ito read over their policies to find out if they do contain such a clause. A great many policies have been lapsed and I think the Minister of Finance should see that this is made a statutory provision in our insurance act.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:

Superannuation - to provide for retiring allowances to former employees of the Department of Public Printing and Stationery, $10,800.
Acoording to the newspapers, an investigation is being carried on with the object of reducing the cost of operating this department; could the minister tell us just what results have been obtained?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think the item refers to
superannuation.

It refers to the Department of Public Printing and Stationery. I understand a subcommittee has been appointed to look into the expenditures of this department in order to see if any economies could be practised.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: A committee was appointed but it was not appointed for the purpose of inquiring into the printing department, it was appointed with a .view to studying the use of printed matter in all departments and the uses to which government publications have been put. The idea was to see if a saving in cost could not be brought about without impairing the efficiency of the service rendered. I understand that committee is doing very excellent work and I hope that it will be possible to effect a very substantial saving in the public service without any disadvantage to the public generally.

My recollection is that the
superannuation act reads, "The governor in council may make payments." It is not obligatory that the payments shall be made and, as I understand it, a civil servant has no absolute statutory right to a pension. I
cannot understand why the act is worded in this way, unless it be to have the pensions freed from tax.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The word "may" has been construed as "shall" on all occasions. Where a public servant is dismissed for malfeasance or misfeasance, discretion may be used but that is the only limitation in connection with superannuation.

What about dismissals for
political partisanship?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I do not know of any person entitled to a pension who has been dismissed for partisanship.

There have been a large
number of dismissals by the present government for this cause and I was wondering if a precedent was being established to be followed by other governments.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I do not think any prospective pensioner has been dismissed for partisanship.

But if he were dismissed,
would he lose his pension?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada

Unforeseen expenses, expenditure thereof to be subject to the approval of the treasury board, and a detailed statement to be laid before parliament within fifteen days of next session, $80,000.

What is included in this
item?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This item is the usual provision for expenditures of an unforeseen character, all payments being subject to the approval of the treasury board. The items vary from year to year. In 1927-28, which was the highest year, the expenditure rose to

Supply-Finance-Miscellaneous
$131,000, and in 1928-29 it was down to $70,000. The amounts vary. Let me give some cases in point. The city taxes on the British legation property in Ottawa are paid under this item. This is a matter of reciprocal arrangement between Canada and the mother country. The British exchequer pays the taxes on the Canadian High Commissioner's office in London and we pay the taxes on the property of the British legation here. As the committee knows, Sir Josiah Stamp refused to accept any payment or salary for the work he did here and the sterling silver candelabra which was presented to him in appreciative testimony of that work was purchased under this item.
I might save the minister some time. I wanted to find out whether this covered miscellaneous items of that nature.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

If so, I do not want to trouble him to read all the other items, being anxious to save a couple of minutes so that the committee may allow me to bring up one matter which might be considered under this item. I refer to the provision of a clothing allowance for pensioners who are receiving relief from the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment. According to a letter that I have received from a pensioner on relief residing in my constituency, it seems that in Calgary pensioners who are on relief are getting a clothing allowance, but pensioners who live in the country do not receive any. I should like to take two or three minutes of the time of the committee to bring up this matter This is a copy of a letter written by this man to Major Bell in Calgary. He says:
Dear Sir,-
Re our conversation, on the 13th instant in your office regarding the department's ruling, that pensioners, who are receiving D.S.C.R. relief, and residing in rural areas, are not eligible to receive clothing, similar to what is being issued to pensioners that are receiving D.S.C.R. relief, and who are residing in the city of Calgary.
It seems strange, pensioners, that are drawing D.S.C.R. relief should be considered, they do not need clothing in the rural areas like brother pensioners who reside in the city of Calgary.
This ruling, though harsh, to the pensioner affected, must strike his sense of humour; -when he remembers a little while ago the government placed 1,000 Doukhobors in jail, for running around in their birthday suits.
I am wondering they didn't send them to the rural areas where clothing is not considered necessary, by at least one department of the government.
He goes on to point out that he has not only himself, but his wife and daughter to clothe.

It seems very strange that a department of the government should be giving clothing allowance in connection with relief which they extend to pensioners in the cities and refuse to accord the same treatment to pensioners in rural areas.
As I believe the estimates of the Department of Pensions are pretty nearly through, I am taking this opportunity of discussing this matter. The Minister of Finance in the final analysis has to decide whether money will be granted to clothe these people or whether they will be sent out to the island on the Pacific coast to live with the Doukobors, and therefore I am simply asking him whether he will give this matter consideration. If he does, I am sure he will give the clothing allowance to pensioners who live in rural areas as well as to those who reside in urban districts. Has the matter been brought to the attention of the minister and, if so, will he give consideration to it and see that the same treatment is accorded to those in the rural areas as is now given to those in the city of Calgary?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
On the hypothesis that
the minister in the last analysis is responsible for the raising of funds for conducting various branches of the public service, my hon. friend could apply to me in regard to every department. I shall take his representations as they appear in Hansard to-morrow and bring them to the attention of my colleague, the Minister of Pensions. I do not know there is any other answer I can give my hon. friend because of course he will understand this is not a question to which I can give any other answer.

I thank the minister for the answer he has given me. I should not have brought this matter up now were it not for the fact I think the estimates of the Department of Pensions are nearly through and I might not have an opportunity to bring it up again. I do not think the government would allow such a condition to continue once it is brought to their attention.

Mr. MARCIL. The two former commissioners have gone?

speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: What gratuity was granted?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Tremblay will receive $5,000 and the other gentleman $2,500.
Why the difference?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
If my memory serves me
correctly it is because of Mr. Tremblay's long service.
They were both appointed at the same time.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
But one had been a long
time in the civil service-twenty-two years, if I remember correctly.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Does the minister believe that is a fair adjustment? After all, a man retired from the public service has still his future to make. It is presumed that if his services are equally satisfactory he should receive an equal gratuity.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
My judgment was not the
deciding factor. In fact, I do not know that I was present when the gratuities were fixed. However the fact is that one has been in the public service a long time, and the opinion of the council was that owing to his longer service the larger amount should be given. Taking into consideration his length of service I believe Mr. Tremblay will not receive a retiring allowance larger than that which would have been proportionate to the longer time he had been in the service.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I was informed both gentlemen were told they would receive the same retirement allowance.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: If the right hon. gentleman wishes the item to stand, I Should be content to agree. I understand however that the House of Commons committee which last session considered civil service matters recommended a larger retirement allowance in one case than in the other.
The minister is absolutely correct.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
I thought so. I understood, further, that the order in council was based upon the report of the committee.
4208	COMMONS
Supply-Civil Service Commission

I notice that savings have been made in a number of items over which the minister has control. I should like to congratulate him upon economizing. However, in view of the financial condition of the country, and in view of the fact that there is a good deal of criticism of this particular branch-

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Is there?

I shall try to show that there
is. In view of those facts, has 'he given any thought to the matter of abolishing altogether the Civil Service Commission, and saving the country about $200,000. At this time that sum of money could be well used, and the people generally would appreciate the saving.
I do not know whether or not the minister has to do with many changes in the public 3ervi.ee, either in regard to appointments or dismissals. Perhaps I am correct when I state that there is no department of government in connection with which there are so few changes as in the department now before the committee. It is a well known fact, however, that in other departments many changes take place. Not only are there thousands of dismissals, but there are thousands of appointments.
In my opinion the Civil Service Commission is nothing more or less than the fifth wheel of a coach. In nine-tenths of the appointments by the Civil Service Commission they act only as rubber stamps. The minister of the department, on the advice of perhaps a member of parliament or his deputy, suggests an appointment to the Civil Service Commission which, in turn, makes the appointment. Let us take an example. We will suppose a postmaster is to be appointed. Quite true, in connection with those appointments there is not only a good deal of red tape but considerable expense. The Civil Service Commission is asked by the Post Office Department to advertise for applicants. The commission sits down seriously and sends out notices to different postmasters, with instructions to post the notices up so that applicants may have an opportunity to apply. All applications are received in Ottawa. Immediately the Post Office Department-not the Civil Sendee Commission-recommends to the Civil Service Commission a number of people who are to act as a board to inquire into the qualifications of the candidates. That is another unnecessary expense. I have known cases where officials have been sent all the way from Ottawa either to British Columbia or the maritime provinces to investigate the qualifications of a postmaster or lighthouse

keeper. They go down with certain instructions. They look over the list of applicants and come back and report to the minister. I have no hesitation in saying that in nine appointments out of ten the member of parliament influences the minister and the minister influences the particular member of the government, the particular member of the government tells the Civil Service Commission who they want appointed and the Civil Service Commission recommends that appointment. I am not criticizing it; I am all for it; I think it is the proper thing, except that it should not go through the Civil Service Commission. I say to the minister that if there is a vacancy in his constituency he is the proper man to make the appointment.
Hear, hear.

I say to every hon. member, if there is a postmaster or lighthouse keeper to be appointed in his constituency he is better qualified to choose that man than three men in the Civil Service Commission who are perhaps two or three thousand miles away from where this man is to be appointed. I have always taken the ground that the Civil Service Commission is a useless piece of machinery. I have no objection to the commissioners themselves; I have no quarrel with the officials, but in the interests of the country the business would be much better carried out by the recommendation of candidates to vacancies by the member of parliament or the defeated candidate than by having all this red tape which does not mean anything. These commissioners really do not make the appointment ; all they do is to put the matter through after either the minister or the officials in certain departments make the recommendation.

My hon. friend from An-tigonish-Guysborough (Mr. Duff) has spoken about boards going around the country to inquire into the qualifications of applicants. They have a simpler method than that in the Post Office Department. They ask the inspector of the district to send one of his assistants to the constituency, and he is told beforehand the name of the man who is to be appointed to that office. So he goes through the formality of giving a rating to the different candidates, and the man to be appointed naturally gets the highest rating. The Civil Service Commission, who have no officials of their own, must trust to the department, and they simply rubber stamp the recommendation and appoint this man who has the highest rating. I could keep this house for two or

Supply-Civil Service Commission
three hours if I wanted to scan the fifty or sixty dismissals which have occurred in my county and which really make the Civil Service Commission as it works at present a perfect farce and a great expense to the country.

If the minister wishes to reply I do not want to take any time. I am opposed to this item, and have been for many years; therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough, that item No. 14 be reduced by $100,000.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
With regard to the Civil Service Commission, the Secretary of State occupies an irresponsible position. I think his sole responsibility is to place the estimates of the commission before the house, and he is the medium through which the commission report to parliament from year to year.
With regard to the dismissals for partisanship or other matters, I can simply say that I am not responsible for any dismissals as far as I know. There has been no dismissal in any branch of the department of the Secretary of State or in any of the departments for which the Secretary of State is responsible as minister. Further I may say that in respect of the appointments that have been made by the Civil Service Commission I certainly have never been consulted in any particular. Consequently the only recommendation I have given to the commission is a personal recommendation as to character for one of the employees of the department of the Secretary of State with whom I had been in close contact for two or three years, whom I believed to be a man of very high character, and when he applied for promotion in the civil service I wrote a certificate as to his character and industry and competence. That is the only association which I have had personally with the commission.

It does seem as if it ought not to be necessary every session, and sometimes two or three times during a session, to debate this question of the Civil Service Commission. I think perhaps the only good thing which can be said with regard to the speech of the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) was that it was short. I have no desire to make a long speech or go into the merits of the case at any length to-day. Yet I think those of us who are in favour of a civil service commission cannot let a protest of this kind go unchallenged. Surely if there is anything wrong with the Civil Service Commission and the way in which they do business
the necessary action is either to bring in amendments to the Civil Service Act or to change the commissioners. I do think that the government is very slack indeed in not having appointed new members to the commission-
Perhaps they have no applicants.

The Civil Service Commission was more or less discredited by a report that came in last session, yet the same gentlemen have carried on, and apparently there has been no fundamental change in their way of doing business. I think the government have been very slack in that connection.
But when we consider the alternative, if the Civil Service Commission were abolished it would mean a return to patronage in a larger degree than we have had it during the past few years. It seems to me that no one who has the welfare of the country at heart can advocate that in real seriousness. I cannot think that any member of parliament, even though he may be located near the scene of action, is necessarily the man to decide who is the most suitable applicant for a position. In fact I think the very fact that he is the member of parliament and is necessarily more or less partisan in his way of looking at things disqualifies him from making recommendations as to the fitness of candidates. I think that position can be well argued. He may know the moral character of a man in his district and may make a recommendation of that kind-
Will the hon. member permit a question? Does not the hon. member frequently make recommendations to the Civil Service Commission?
No, I do not.

Have you never made
any?

No, I have not,
that is to the best of my knowledge.

To the best of your
knowledge?

Yes, I cannot recall at any time having done so. As everyone here knows, I have said again and again that I believe in the principle of appointment on merit after competitive examination, and I have referred applicants to the Civil Service 'Commission, but not with recommendations.
4210	COMMONS
Supply-Civil Service Commission

Then may I ask
another question? The hon. member says that in all his career as a member of this house, and he has been here many years, he has never made a recommendation to the Civil Service Commission?

I cannot recall any. I am not under examination, and before making a final statement I would have to be given time to go over the matter. The nearest I can recall to having done anything of the kind was away out in the west, not in my own constituency, when either a minister or the Civil Service Commission asked me if I could indicate some medical man who could recommend someone upon whom reliance could be placed, and I indicated a medical man that I happened to know in that area, and I do not know who he recommended. To the best of my knowledge that is the nearest I have come to any recommendation.
Then may I ask this question? In all his career the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has never made any recommendation to the Civil Service Commission?
To the best of my knowledge, no.
Your knowledge and belief?
Not to the best of my recollection.
I am prepared to leave it at that.

If sworn evidence were brought in I might have to accept my own signature, or other evidence like that, but my statement is according to the best of my recollection. I am dealing with principles, and on principle I have avoided doing that. It may be that those of us who are independents are not subjected to quite the same temptations as others; I am not suggesting that I possess any higher degree of morality, but perhaps I occupy rather a unique position. That has been the position I have taken, and perhaps for that very reason I have been able to advocate the retention and extension of the Civil Service Commission a little more disinterestedly than some other hon. members. I felt very sorry that the appointments recently made in connection with the radio commission did not come under the Civil Service Commission, so far as I have been able to learn, but were made directly by order in council. If I am misinformed I should be very glad to be corrected.
That is quite right.

I think that is correct, and it is regrettable indeed. By these means we are really undermining the authority and usefulness of the Civil Service Commission, and if this undermining goes on very much longer I might come to agree with my hon. friend from Antigonish-Guysborough and regard the commission as a fifth wheel. But I do not want to see it made a fifth wheel; I think we need an independent body who will have some definite knowledge of the qualifications of individuals and of the needs of the departments, and I hope nothing further will be done to weaken the Civil Service Commission. If this amendment is pressed I shall have to vote against it.

In addition to what I said a moment ago with regard to appointments in the country districts, section 25 of the Civil Service Act enables the department to accept or reject the recommendation of the Civil Service Commission, and when by any accident a Liberal is appointed that recommendation is rejected. I have a case in point in my own constituency. A returned soldier was appointed as lighthouse keeper; he was the father of a fairly large family. This did not suit the Tory organization and the appointment was held up for six months. The temporary appointee received his salary during that period, and when the six months was up the choice of the Tory organizer in my constituency was appointed. The returned soldier, who had been legally appointed by the commission, was simply thrown aside. The recommendation of the Civil Service Commission was completely annulled under section 25 of the act, which enables the department to accept or refuse any appointment. When the appointee does not suit the men of the day he is not accepted; in this case the soldier who had been appointed was simply thrown out.

I do not see that the hon. member for Bonaventure has very much to complain about. During the ten years his party was in power that section was invoked day in and day out in order to get rid of candidates who had received the highest rating by the Civil Service Commission. If the hon. gentleman wants to refresh his memory let him look at the debates of 1930, when the post office estimates were under consideration. My complaint against the Civil Service Commission is that at times they allow themselves to be influenced by others, and the merit system is not always to the fore. If the hon. gentleman wants a concrete illustration let him look at the case of the Camp-bellton postmaster.

Supply-Civil Service Commission

I had nothing to do with that; I only know that an appointment was made by the Civil Service Commission and that now an attempt i3 being made to have that cancelled. Of the one hundred postmasters in my constituency I think about fifty have been dismissed. The other day a man was dismissed by the Postmaster General despite a fervent appeal made on his behalf by the Lord Bishop of Quebec. Mr. Sweet-man, the postmaster in question, who had held office for thirty-four years at Port Daniel Centre, and who was kept in office under the Borden government by Sir Robert Borden himself when an attempt was made to oust him, has been let out. I am in favour of merit, but the merit system does not work properly. All the government officials are trembling with regard to their positions. If a post office inspector is sent down to my district, what does he do?- The easiest way is for him to see the member who has the patronage for the county. In my case my opponent does not bother with patronage; he has passed it over to a former minister of the crown, Hon. Doctor Paquet, who was a member of the Meighen administration. He is handling the patronage now, and this dismissal was carried out on the recommendation of Doctor Paquet in spite of the appeal of the Lord Bishop of Quebec, who I am sure could be compared with Doctor Paquet any day of the week.
I could bring up any number of similar instances. These things are done for party purposes; I have sat here for thirty-three years, and I know what I am talking about. When my hon. friend from York-Sunbury goes back to his people he will have to account for the expenditures of the present government. I know he has a pretty safe constituency, but he may find that conditions have changed, and that the people are in earnest. They may want to know if only individuals and private companies should economize or whether the Dominion government should not set the example. I am sure my hon. friend and I could sit down and reduce the budget by millions of dollars. Many things are all right when the country is prosperous; it is all right to have representation at Geneva and elsewhere and commissioners galore when the country has money, but I think we could get along without a lot of these things now. Here we have a tax of 2 cents a pound on sugar; we have to put 3 cents on every cheque no matter how small it may be; we must raise $70,000,000 by increased taxation this year. At the same time the trade of Canada for the
month of March was $28,000,000 less than our trade a year ago, and I do not know how many millions less than our trade in 1928 and 1929. So I think the time has come when we must economize, and I am in favour of abolishing the Civil Service Commission entirely, so far as the outside service is concerned. Let the minister of the crown assume the responsibility for appointments, and let him make those appointments on the recommendation of the man who has been chosen to represent the people of that constituency. If I make a foolish appointment I am responsible first to the minister and then to my electors. Then the minister will have someone to whom he can look with confidence, because I must assume the responsibility, as every member of parliament must. That is the way the civil service should be administered, but to-day we have this costly farce, the Civil Service Commission. It gives no satisfaction to anyone; the appointments are made purely for party purposes, and in each case a large number of good partisans are dissatisfied. If you want to get into trouble, change a post office; that is the old story, and my hon. friend knows it very well. I know my hon. friend is sincere; he knows in his heart that we could save millions of dollars if we really wanted to do so. We should cut our budget down to compare with our revenues, but here we are this year with a deficit of $150,000,000. What is to become of this country if trade does not pick up or if something is not done at Washington or some other place? Where will we be in the next two or three years? I put that question to my hon. friend, and he will have an opportunity to answer it.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: A moment ago the Secretary of State said that he, as a minister of the crown, had never asked the Civil Service Commission to make an appointment.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Or as a private member, so far as I know.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: And that the only action he had taken along that line was to give a certificate of character to someone who was seeking a position.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: And in that case the gentleman had been in the State department under me, where I had been able to supervise his competency and intelligence. I do not think he has received the appointment, at that.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Quite so, and I think in making that statement the minister felt that he was expressing the proper



Supply-Civil Service Commission
attitude of a minister of the crown with reference to appointments under the Civil Service Commission. A few days ago we were discussing in the house a measure which related to the appointment of wardens in penitentiaries, and the Minister of Justice at the time told us that one reason a certain clause in the act had been drafted as it was was to remove altogether the possibility of the minister making the recommendation for the appointment of wardens. He said that it would be better to leave the matter in the hands of the superintendent and that the minister should not interfere at all. We accepted in good faith what the minister then said. I have in my hand a return asked for a few days ago by the hon. member for South Perth (Mr. Sanderson) and I wish to read to the committee two or three of the communications that appear therein. They illustrate to what extent the Civil Service Commission really functions in the matter of some appointments. This return relates to the appointment of a warden at Kingston. The motion asked for:
A copy of all correspondence, telegrams, recommendations, reports, memoranda and other documents on the files of the Minister _ of Justice, the Solicitor General and of the Civil Service Commission in respect to the appointment of K. M. Allan to the position of warden of Collin's Bay penitentiary.
The first letter is dated Ottawa, January 14, 1932. This is a memorandum signed by the Minister of Justice and forwarded to the superintendent of penintentiaries:
Please instruct Inspector Jackson to return to his regular duties at Ottawa as inspector, and place Mr. Allan in charge of the preferred class penitentiary, Collin's Bay, as acting warden. Please also apply to the Civil Service Commission for the promotion of Mr. Allan to be warden of said institution, and for the promotion of Mr. Hawkins to the position now occupied by Mr. Allan.
That was a pretty straight statement on the part of the Minister of Justice as to what the Civil Service Commission should do. Then there is a communication from Mr. W. S. Hughes, superintendent, to Mr. Allan. It is dated January 18, 1932:
Dear Mr. Allan,-
Acting under instructions of the hon. the Minister of Justice, you are to proceed immediately to the preferred class penitentiary, Collins bay, and take charge of that institution.
That communication is addressed to:
R. M. Allan, Esq., Structural Engineer, Penitentiary Branch, Ottawa.

On January 21, 1932, there is quite a long letter from the Deputy Minister of Justice, addressed to the Secretary of the Civil Service Commission, Ottawa. It reads in part:
Sir,-
Re-Promotion, Structural Engineer R. M. Allan, J.PA. 17, to position, warden, grade 1, preferred class penitentiary, Collin's Bay, J.P. 2001.
Relative to the above, the position of warden at the preferred class penitentiary, Collins bay, has not been permanently filled since its creation. The hon. the Minister of Justice is desirous of having the above mentioned officer promoted to this vacancy.
Then the communication gives certain reasons and concludes:
May I ask that steps be taken to immediately promote Mr. Allan to the permanent position of warden of the preferred class penitentiary, at the salary he now enjoys, viz., $3,180. The customary requisition is attached hereto.
I am, sir,

There is the file. I have not read all the communications but the pertinent ones, and I have not left unread any communications which hon. gentlemen would wish to have quoted. That file indicates that in the filling of positions such as that of warden, the Minister of Justice simply told the superintendent whom he wanted appointed. He had his deputy write to the Civil Service Commission, indicating who was to be appointed, the Civil Service Commission made the appointment, and the superintendent notified this gentleman that the appointment had been made. If that is the method of proceeding under the present government, so far as the Civil Service Commission is concerned, the motion before the committee at the moment is wholly inadequate. Instead of reducing the salaries paid to the commission we ought to abolish it altogether. This is the file as presented and I shall be glad to send it over to my hon. friend if he wishes to see it. It is an exemplification of what wre on this side have been

saying, that so far as the Civil Service Commission is concerned, as apparently it is functioning at the present time, it is simply acting under instructions from the minister, the minister giving directions to his head officials or his deputy and, through them, instructing the commission what to do.

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext:
It seems to me
the right hon. gentleman has taken too highhanded an attitude in this matter. As a matter of fact, these are not instructions to the commission at all. The commission are not bound to carry out the wishes of the minister.
But they did.

speechtext:
They axe not
bound to carry out these instructions unless they see fit, and my experience of the commission is that anyone whom I recommend very seldom gets any consideration. Indeed, I no longer recommend anyone to the commission. The minister or the deputy minister might say that he would like to have such a man appointed, but that does not constitute instructions to the commission. If the commission refused to appoint the man the minister could not compel them to make the appointment.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Will the Acting Prime Minister listen to this.

They considered

speechtext: "May I ask that steps be -taken" cannot be regarded as instructions. As a matter of fact, the minister could not instruct the commission if he wished to.

I can understand that the Acting Prime Minister would not wish to have very much to do with the Civil Service Commission, nor would he ask them to make appointments, but he is a member of this government and he cannot get away from some responsibility in the matter. I will refer to one case that occurred in the last couple of months. A radio commission was appointed and it was found necessary to have certain officials. The commission asked for a secretary, and although the commission was requested to advertise 53719-266 J
for applicants for that position, although two hundred applications were received by the commission, although these poor devils of applicants each paid $2 when he sent in his application, the appointment of Colonel Landry was made the day before the applications were due. Who made that appointment? Was it made without the advice of the Civil Service Commission? Was the Civil Service Commission not told to appoint that gentleman instead of one of the two hundred applicants who sent in 82 each, and from whom the government derived S400?

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: This is something I know nothing about. Does my hon friend say that the appointment was made the day before the applications were received?
Before they were due.

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: Before they were received?
No, before the time was up.

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: Has the hon. gentleman anything to prove that?
The Acting Prime Minister can get the proof better than I can. I would suggest that he ask his colleagues.

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: I ask the hon. gentleman whether he has any written evidence.
I have made the statement that this was done and I would suggest that the Acting Prime Minister make an investigation Let him ask his colleagues whether it is true or not.

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: I will have the matter investigated.

My views with reference to the Civil Service Commission are well known to all members of the committee and I do not propose to repeat them at this moment. I have had occasion time and time again to express my views and they will be found in Hansard. I have agreed in the past with the principles underlying the Civil Service Commission, and I repeat my agreement. I agree with the principle of having a body to appoint people to the civil service under the merit system. If there are any defects in this system, it is not due so much to those charged with the administration of the law as it is to the law itself. If a change were made in the act in an impartial manner and irrespective of parties and the like, a lot of the trouble now being experienced would be removed. I am one of those who believe in the merit system and I see no other way
