in which it can be administered except by a properly constituted commission operating under a proper law. I notice there is a reduction of almost S50.000 in the vote for this commission. I shall not repeat what I have said before, but notwithstanding my great friendship for the hon. gentleman who has moved that the item be reduced, I shall very gladly vote against his amendment.
Would the hon. gentleman tell us how many recommendations he has made to the Civil Service Commission between 1921 and 1930 and how many times he has tried to influence appointments?

When anyone came to me and asked me to recommend him to the Civil Service Commission, I did so when I felt that he wag worthy of appointment. However, I might say that as far as I know, not one of these applications has been accepted. Since the change in government, people have come to me asking me to recommend them for positions. As my hon. friend knows, the application form contains a space for three recommendations. Since 1930 I have been quite willing to place my name upon the application forms of those whom I thought were fitted for positions, but not one of them has been appointed.

I should like to bring a matter to the attention of both the Secretary of State (Mr. Cahan) and the Minister of the Interior. A gentleman in my county acted as chief migratory bird officer for over nine years in the province of Prince Edward Island. It was decided to hand this work over to the mounted police and this man's name was placed upon the eligible fist of the Civil Service Commission. Just recently the position of fishery officer in my county became vacant, a position which entails work similar to that which this man had done. When the natural resources were handed over to the provinces, many positions in the Department of the Interior were wiped out, but the minister knows it was intended that these men would be taken care of. This man to whom I refer is a returned soldier and I think the minister will bear me out when I say that he had a splendid record with the department. The Civil Service Commission was about to advertise the position of fishery officer when this man put forward the claim that as he was on the eligible list, he should receive the appointment. The commission agreed with this, but in order that this man should not receive the position an order in council was passed stating that it would not be filled in

a permanent way. A couple of days afterwards another man was put into this position upon the recommendation of the gentleman who opposed me in the last election. A man who had been in the department for nearly ten years was passed over although the commission had admitted that he was eligible for the position and should receive it. I do not know whether this man was a Liberal or a Conservative, I just want to point out that there are many ways of getting around the act. This man was wounded in service overseas, he has given splendid sendee in the department but he is now thrown out in the cold simply because someone else wants to place another man in the position. The Civil Service Commission were ready to appoint this man and I have their letter to prove it.

May I point

pect that any federal officer should have anything to do with supervising the accounts of the provinces. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The position taken by the Prime Minister to which my right hon. friend has referred, had reference to the auditing of the accounts which are paid for in part by the provinces themselves and which are administered and dealt with by the provinces, whereas on the other hand the letter of the Prime Minister had reference not to the creation of accounts but to the question of requests which have come to the dominion for advances, loans and financial aid to enable the provinces to carry out their own provincial undertakings. It all relates

Yes. On the other hand,
the lender is the man who lays down the terms on which the borrower is to receive an advance.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
My point is
that at the outset the government should not have regarded it as an insult to. the provinces to lay down any terms. We were taking the very strong position that being the lender, the federal government ought to safeguard the dominion treasury in its loans. Had that course been taken, the position of the provinces to-day would not have been the difficult one it is; it would not have been necessary to tell them that the time had come when they had better get a comptroller or they would not get help.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not think there is any difference in view between my right hon. friend and myself except that he is confusing two things. The question of auditing accounts as approved by a province where the province itself administers and pays a portion of them is one thing, while the question of the federal government saying to a province which comes to the dominion treasury requesting the loan of a certain sum of money:	Yes, we will lend you the money,
but on condition that you will do thus and so, is entirely different.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: If we are agreed, I am satisfied.

The answer to the minister
by the provinces would be this, that if the federal government had not initiated these enormous expenditures, the provinces might not have been in the difficult position in which they are. If they are asking for money to assist in carrying out certain undertakings under a relief act, it is because they were obliged to make these expenditures. The federal government simply said:	We will
spend so much and you must also spend so much; if you do not, you are to be held up before the inhabitants of your province as not being willing to cooperate with us. The provinces have been actually forced into the expenditure of large sums of money.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I cannot allow the statement of my hon. friend to pass without a moderate protest.
I did not expect the minister would.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It may quite well be that the dominion must assume a share of responsibility for certain public works expenditures which were participated in by the provinces and that to the exent they did participate in certain public works expenditures, there may have resulted a modicum of financial embarrassment at the moment. That may have been a contributing cause, but it was not by any stretch of the imagination the main cause of the difficulty in which the several western provinces find themselves at present. One must go far beyond that for many of the expenditures that they are called upon to make to-day. When I say that, I am not referring to parliament buildings which cost many millions of dollars and other undertakings of a like character which at the time were beyond the purse of the provinces to meet. Let me take one illustration. In the drought area in Saskatchewan, there was a case where one-third of the population of that province was impoverished, not in a position to pay a single dollar of taxation and, on the other hand, having to be the recipients of direct relief to the extent of one hundred per cent. That one instance alone would cause a diminution in the revenue of Saskatchewan of a very large sum of money. Then, of course, the provinces are also subject to the general conditions of depression which exist to-day.

speechtext: Building fishways and clearing rivers, $18,000.

Mr. Chairman, I note that
this item is for clearing rivers and building fish ladders. There is a lake in my district which requires a fish ladder. As I understand it, sockeye salmon eggs were put into that lake four years ago, and the run is due to come back this fall. I have made inquiries from the department, and learn that the proposal is to wait until they come back, and then to think about building a ladder. That may seem reasonable to the department; they may choose to adopt that course rather than to build a ladder before the run. But the history of the Pacific coast tells us that if we put sockeye eggs into a lake we can count on it that they will return four years after. The department states there is a precedent in connection with Stamp falls, in which instance they waited until the run came back. In that case however the falls were not of a character which made the ascent of the fish prohibitive. Those falls only made it difficult for the fish to get up, and their efforts were supplemented through provision by the department to carry them up a distance of perhaps a couple of hundred yards in some kind of pail or bucket. Out of a fairly prolific run one could imagine how many would ascend in that way. The efforts of the department were of course supplemented by the fact that the falls were not impossible of ascent, and that at least to a certain extent the fish could get up in any event.
In the particular instance to which I allude, however, I am advised the fall is much deeper, about fifteen feet straight down, and that it would be impossible for fish to get up unless a fish way were built, or some blasting done. I am not asking for a large expenditure, but I do say a little blasting would make it possible for the fish to get up. But expensively to propagate fish, to wait for four years until they come back, and then to carry them up in a bucket, does seem a waste of public money. How many of a run could be taken up in that way? The sockeye salmon is a fairly large fish weighing ten or twelve pounds and in my view the government would be well advised to spend money preparing the falls so that the fish may get up in the natural way. Some preparation of that type would not cost any more than carrying the fish by hand, and the result would be that all the

Supply-Fisheries
fish, rather than one per cent, would get up. The particular place I have in mind, one with which the minister's deputy is familiar, is Maggie lake.

I should like to ask the government when a Minister of Fisheries is going to be appointed. I am willing to admit that my good friend the Minister of Marine and acting Minister of Fisheries is a very oapable minister of the crown, but there is no question that the .Canadian fisheries, being a very important industry, require a minister of their own. Since my good friend the Minister of Finance was promoted to that responsible position, there has been no minister of fisheries. I should like to know if the minister or the government could tell the committee when a minister of fisheries is to be appointed. I suggest of course that the appointment should go to the maritime provinces. Further than that, I suggest it should be given to the province of Nova Scotia. While the Minister of Finance represents that province, and is a very estimable gentleman indeed, yet with his great responsibilities as Minister of Finance he cannot be expected to look after the fisheries. I should like to know what the government is contemplating in this connection.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The hon. member for
AntigoniSh-Guysborough, with his knowledge of parliamentary practice, will appreciate at once that any answer to his question could be given only by the Prime Minister, whose prerogative it is to select the members of his
administration. The only answer I can give is to say that upon 'the Prime Minister's return I shall direct his attention to the remarks of the hon. member.

Everybody knows that politically I am not a very good friend of the Prime Minister, but I must take issue with the Minister of Finance when he throws responsibility for the present vacancy in the Department of Fisheries on the shoulders of my good friend the Prime Minister. A short time ago the Minister of Marine was asked with regard to the appointment of a deputy minister of marine. On that occasion he, too, passed the buck very nicely, stating that he could not give any information to the house with regard to the appointment of a deputy minister of marine, because it was a matter purely within the control of the Prime Minister. Of course it is quite possible that in the final analysis the Prime Miinster has to sign his name on the dotted line, whether the appointment be that of a minister or of a deputy minister. I understand that the Prime Minister has the entree to His Excellency the Governor General, and I presume that when an appointment is made of so important a character as that of Minister of Fisheries, His Excellency will see only the Prime Minister. Nevertheless other ministers of the crown have certain responsibilities in regard to this important vacancy. Again I say that the fisheries of this country is a very important matter, not only to the Atlantic coast and the Pacific coast but also to the district of the great lakes. I say it is not fair to the people interested in that great industry that this post should be vacant for such a long time. I see just coming to his seat my good friend the minister without portfolio from Prince Edward Island (Mr. Macdonald). He is a member of this government, without portfolio it is true; but if in the wisdom of the government someone should recommend that that hon. member be appointed as minister with portfolio, as far as I am concerned I should be very glad to say amen to that appointment. But surely the present situation is not fair to the Minister of Marine (Mr. Duranleau) who has grave responsibilities regarding his own department; for he has the Gibb report on his hands-such a weighty matter that he cannot decide what to do with it this session and it is to be held over. Looking at him now one can see that he has a number of responsibilities. He also has had to put over the shipping bill; he has so many other matters that he cannot deal with it this session. Why should this minister be loaded up with another depart-

ment which needs the attention of a man with special qualifications to look after this great industry, one of the foremost we have, an industry which 'has never cost the country very much, and which is always bringing new money to the country. I say that this government should decide immediately to appoint a minister of fisheries. I do not want to embarrass any more of my hon. friends on the other side, but may I say this-and I am glad the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis (Mr. Short) is not here: if the Minister of Finance will take my advice, if he does not want to relieve the present minister without portfolio from Prince Edward Island of his present position, then I say he has in the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis a man well qualified for the office of Minister of Fisheries. I strongly recommend that something be done to fill this position, which has been vacant since my hon. friend the Minister of Finance was elevated to the exalted position he now occupies.

that the expenditure for expanding the demand for fish covers the whole of Canada. The work has been carried on from ocean to ocean. And if there are other urgent demands on the western coast the vote is not especially for the east, it is for the whole of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: I have not the exact figure, but I know that Mrs. Spencer was on the Pacific coast for more than two months last winter, during January and February and part of March.

But even she would not account for S75,000. The minister has practically admitted that almost all this money was spent in the east, and I am not grudging it; if it was needed there it should have been spent there. That brings me to the consideration of another feature, however, and I am sorry my hon. friend from Digby-Anna-polis is not here to-night; I know he would support me.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: There was no admission of the kind made by the minister.

It was a tacit admission. I did not expect the minister to say it in so many words; that would be expecting too much of human nature. This brings me to the consideration of an item in connection with which I have made an annual protest for some years. I hope perhaps this will be the last time I will have to bring it up because I have a premonition, which other people might call a hunch, that my protest will prevail this time. I refer to the allocation, or the lack of allocation, of the $160,000 granted annually for fisheries bounties. On this occasion I am more confident of success, though I always have had justice, equity and law on my side. The hon. member for Digby-Annapolis and the hon. member for Cape Breton South always have given me their moral sympathy and admitted I was right, but they have always insisted that because they have had this graft in the past they should continue to have it. No doubt this is the result of some lingering aura of old Scotland hanging around the fogbound coast of Nova Scotia. This year, however, I have a higher authority to call to my support; I refer to the minister himself. On February 27 the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough asked the acting Minister of Fisheries with regard to the fishing bounties, and on that occasion I spoke as follows:
Has the minister considered giving British Columbia and the Pacific coast its share of that fund?
Mr. Duranleau: The money will be divided according to the statute.
That is all I ever asked, that the money should be allocated according to the statute. In years gone by I have found that if you go to a French speaking cabinet minister and get him to promise something, his word is good; forever sacred remains the word of a French speaking minister. In the case of an English
speaking minister I have sometimes found it desirable to call around a few days later to see if he had forgotten about it.
I need not go over the whole question again; the minister and his deputy have all the records before them. This money is voted under a special act, not connected with something else that happened four years before. The act was passed in 1882, if I remember rightly, simply directing that out of the consolidated revenues of Canada the sum of $160,000 should be taken yearly and devoted to the stimulation of the fisheries of Canada. I claim that we are a part of Canada, but we have been neglected, ignored and robbed of our share from 1882 until the present day. I do not wonder that the hon. members to whom I referred are not here tonight. They cannot defend this action; it is indefensible. The Minister of Finance made a stab at it one day, but he could not get away with it. They say that this refers to a transaction under which the United States paid a large sum of money into the consolidated revenue fund of Canada in return for allowing certain fishing privileges to the fishermen of the United States. We are told that when the United States paid that amount the Canadian people surrendered a portion of their privileges, and that was a portion of my privileges as well as the privileges of the people of Nova Scotia. In any ease, Mr. Chairman, the money was paid into the consolidated revenue fund, and there it lost its identity. Several years later, for reasons with which I am not acquainted and with which I am not concerned, the government of Canada decided to vote out of the consolidated revenue fund the sum of $160,000 yearly for the improvement of the fishing industry of Canada. In those days we did not ask our share because we did not have very much in the way of fisheries, but we are here now clamouring for what is rightfully ours. We do not want to go back into the sad past, but we want our share in the future.
If any further reason need be given I will only refer to the way the money is being frittered away now. The Minister of Finance needs money and does not know which way to turn, but here is $160,000 being frittered away in little dabs here and there. One man gets $6.80; another man gets $5.80 and another man $1 a ton on his boat, all for the support and stimulation of the fishing industry. If the money was spent in a reasonable way we would still have a claim to our share. That famous Duncan report particularly said that this method of distributing the money was unfair and useless, and that this was a waste of public money.
Supply-Fisheries

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: Do I understand that my hon. friend's views are that these bounties should not be given?

No, I am not adverse to the spending of the money in a proper manner in order really to stimulate the industry, but I think in whatever way it is spent it should be divided equally between the Pacific and the Atlantic.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: But if it is money wasted on the east coast-
I would not say it was wasted, but we seem to be getting very little for it.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: -would it not be wasted also on the west coast?

I do not understand how giving a man $580 is going to stimulate his interest in the fishing industry. That is what is given each man who goes out in a boat, and that is supposed to stimulate the deep sea fisheries of Canada. I do not know what goes on down there but I do not see how this is calculated to promote the object in view.

I do not want to get into a controversy with my good friend from Comox-Alberni, but evidently he is not acquainted with the facts concerning this vote for bounty purposes and the history surrounding it. In the first place the hon. member said this parliament voted $160,000 each year for bounty purposes. That is not correct; there is no amount voted by this parliament for bounty purposes each year. This is a statutory amount, just as the judges' salaries are statutory. Where does this money come from?
God knows.

God does know, and I am going to tell the committee. This money does not come from the taxpayers of this country; it was paid by the United States in return for certain privileges they obtained along the Atlantic coast. It has nothing at all to do with the Pacific coast. In 1870, if I remember correctly, a commission was appointed to investigate the fisheries of the Atlantic coast, in which the citizens of Canada, the United States and Newfoundland all had certain privileges. That commission decided that $5,000,000, if I remember oorrectly, should be paid by the United States in return for certain privileges, $4,000,000 coming to Canada and 81,000,000 going to Newfoundland. That $4,000,000 has been in the treasury of Canada ever since, and this $160,000, which is never voted by this parliament-
Are you sure of that?

Yes, I am quite sure it is not voted by parliament. The interest on that $4,000,000, at 4 per cent, is set aside because the fishermen of New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island and Gaspe gave certain privileges to our neighbours to the south. It has nothing to do with the Pacific coast. Whether the fishermen of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island or Quebec received $5.80 or $6.80 is irrelevant. This money belongs not to the people of Canada but only to a certain number of them living in certain parts of the country, and so far as the people on the Pacific coast are concerned they have no right to it, nor is it any of their business how the. money is spent. By an arrangement made fifty or sixty years ago it was decided that this money should be divided in two ways: first, by allowing the vessels $1 per ton up to 80 tons, and then by dividing the balance of the $160,000 among the fishermen engaged in the industry in the particular season. Some years they received $6.80 and other years, when there were more fishermen, $5.80 or $5.90. As regards British Columbia however they certainly have no more right to the money than I have to any money voted by the congress of the United States. I cannot understand why my hon. friend from Comox-Alberni should get up and claim that the fishermen of British Columbia or of the great lakes or the fishermen on lake Winnipeg ought to participate in this particular amount which was devoted to a specific purpose.

I admit that the hon. member has done his best, but he has a very poor case to work on. He went back seventy or more years. The money obtained from the United States was I believe $5,000,000 and in 1878 it was placed in the consolidated revenue fund of Canada. The hon. gentleman says that this money was provided as compensation to the fishermen of the maritimes for giving up certain privileges. It was not; it was to provide compensation for the fishermen of Canada. Does he mean to say that if I had gone there in 1882 I should not have been allowed to fish? Of course it would have been my privilege to fish there as it was the privilege of any Canadian. He says we did not vote this money. Well, that is merely a play on words; we voted it in a lump sum in 1882, when the act was passed. The hon. member says it was placed in the consolidated revenue fund in 1878. The hon. gentleman evidently hopes that it is floating around in the consolidated fund to-day. If he can find it there I will give him an equal amount.

Have you got it.

Supply-Fisheries

It was placed in the consolidated revenue fund and it went the way of all consolidated revenue funds. Four years passed and possibly because an election was coming on, who shall say, the parliament of Canada passed what is known as chapter 74 of the revised statutes, the Deep Sea Fisheries Act, which provided that an annual grant- not a bonus but a grant-of $160,000 should be ;aken out of the consolidated revenue fund for the purpose indicated; but there was not a word, not a whisper, not a syllable of reference to the situation which the hon. gentleman has outlined. It was something quite independent of and apart from that. It was said that it was to be used in aid of the sea fisheries of Canada and for the improvement of the conditions of fishermen. What fishermen, pray, and where? The fishermen of Canada. And we, in British Columbia, are part of Canada. The hon. gentleman is inclined to forget that. If you will look at the .aw you will see that they have no right to the whole of the money as that law exists, and as a matter of fact we are deprived of our share simply in consequence of the regulations made by the minister. He could not possibly do it under the act, because the act is quite explicit; it must therefore be done by regulations which the minister is empowered to make. It is a well known principle of law that you can pass regulations only if they amplify the act; you cannot make regulations that constitute another act. But that is what .he minister did from time to time; he made mother act by his regulations. By means of /hose regulations he removed British Columbia from the operation of the act of 1882, and I say he has no power to do that. All that my friends from the maritimes can claim is this. They say, "What the member for Comox-Alberni says is true and legal, but it should not have been done." Possibly it should not have been done, but it was done, and they fall back now on the time-honoured argument that it has always been like this and what we have we will hold. But time does not justify a wrong. I ask the minister, in view of his pronouncement that he would distribute the money in accordance with the act, to take appropriate steps in this matter. Chapter 74 of the revised statutes provides that the money shall be for the benefit of the fishermen of Canada, and as the minister is a new man I should like to hear him say that he will live up to the promise he gave me, as indicated in Hansard of the day I have mentioned, and distribute the money in accordance with the act.

The hon. member for Comox-Alberni says that the act which he has cited provided that the money should be devoted to the fishermen of Canada. What else could it say? It could not pick out one province and declare that the money should be for that province. In these estimates there is $300,000 for fish culture and I have no hesitation in saying that seventy-five per cent of that sum is spent in British Columbia, ostensibly for the benefit of the fisheries of Canada. We are not complaining about that; because $22.5,000 of that $300,000 is spent in British Columbia we are making no complaint, nor should my hon. friend, because of the act which he has referred to, argue that this money was intended for the fisheries of the dominion at large. It could mean any particular part of Canada. Take another illustration. When the Minister of Finance brought down his budget the other day it contained an item with regard to what is known as the stabilization fund, and when inquiry was made as to what that item meant with regard to the fisheries it was shown that practically the only part of Canada that would benefit to the extent of hundreds of thousands was British Columbia. Did my hon. friend from Victoria-Carieton or my hon. friend from Digby-Annapolis object to it? No. Yet my hon. friend now brings forward an act passed fifty years ago to bolster up an argument that cannot hold water. He says that this money provided for the maritimes should also be given in part to British Columbia.
Carried.
May we hear from the minister.
Carried.

No. If we are not going to hear from the minister I take it that his silence is assent to my argument. He has seen the virtue of my argument, and that being settled I will pass on to something else. This item deals with the conservation of fish, and I have had a number of complaints in regard to what is considered the rather too common habit of dumping fish. We know we spend enormous sums of money, running into millions of dollars, for the preservation and conservation of fish. I have letters here, from one of which I will quote:
In connection with the dumping of edible salmon back into the water, we wish to draw your attention to such a condition in this district.
In this district a cannery wanting_ cohoe for canning has been sending out boats' with instructions to bring in only cohoe and a limited number of bright chums, with the natural result
Supply-Fisheries

that hundreds of salmon have been caught, picked over, and then the poorer ones turned back into the water where they w'ill die as they cannot survive the handling. In one case we know of several hundred chums being thrown away because it did not suit the convenience of the company to handle them though they were prime fish.
On another occasion, it is alleged, twelve thousand fish were dumped overboard by one cannery. There does not seem to be any provision in the act or in the regulations to guard against such a thing. I have a letter from the department in which it is stated that the practice cannot be stopped. The letter reads in part as follows:
If salmon caught in conformity with the regulations do happen to be dumped, the occurrence, however regrettable from the standpoint of wastage, does not contravene such conservation regulations.
It may not contravene the regulations but I contend that a man who proposes to dump ten or twelve thousand salmon should be forced to notify the fisheries officials and obtain their consent. Although it would not be in conformity with the act, it might be possible that arrangements could be made so that the fish could be disposed of to a reduction plant and thereby not be a total loss. If my suggestion were carried out the officials would be advised as to the amount of dumping and if a certain individual or cannery was dumping too many fish, discrimination could be carried out in the matter of granting them licences. Until I notified the department they had not the slightest idea that this practice was being carried on. I submit that there should be some attempt made to keep a check upon this dumping. If sufficient publicity were given, the practice would be discontinued because these men would not care to have their names appear too often upon a blacklist. If they did persist in the practice, they could be penalized when licences were being granted.
While I am on my feet I should like to refer to another matter. Last fall I applied to the department for permission for the unemployed of Courtenay to take pinks out of the river. This is a second-class fish which was selling at two cents apiece at that time, but my request was turned down. I was told that the guardians would have sufficient common sense not to interfere with anyone taking fish for food. That is all very well, but these junior men feel that they must live up to their instructions. The result was that the poor of the town of Courtenay were not able to go out and jig a few fish for their own use. The amount they would have taken would not have been a fleahite as far as

conservation was concerned. We all know how sensitive people are when they are down and out and forced to rely on relief. These men who were not permitted to go out and catch a few fish for their own use heard of this dumping of nine or ten thousand fish. Such things make for discontent. I suggest that the department should endeavour to keep itself informed on these matters and see that a close check is kept.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: I will take note of the suggestion my hon. friend has made and if it is necessary to adopt more strict regulations, they will be adopted.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Fish culture, $300,000.

Why is the west coast of Vancouver island not getting some Atlantic salmon? The experts say that the lakes and creeks of the west coast of Vancouver island cannot be surpassed for the propagation of Atlantic salmon. In these hard times I was quite prepared to be told that our day would come, but I was rather surprised to see in one of the bulletins issued by the department that Atlantic salmon eggs have been shipped to the state of California. Are not the waters of Abana and Pharpar greater than the muddy waters of the Jordan? Are not the waters of the west coast of Vancouver island as important as those of the state of California? I know the argument will be used that these eggs were sent on an exchange basis, that we received from the state of California a certain quantity of steelheads, but it must be remembered that steelheads are almost of no commercial use. They are nothing more or less than a sport trout and the commercial use of the fish would not be more than one per cent of the total catch. If we had Atlantic salmon on the west coast of the island we could develop a considerable tourist trade. We have lost the advantage of liquor, but we still have our scenery and climate, and Atlantic salmon would bring people from all over the world. I think we should come before the state of California and I should like to know why it was thought advisable to ship eggs to that state when the west coast of the island could not be supplied.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: I am told by my officials that we have been sending Atlantic salmon to the Pacific coast for years but it has not proved successful.

I am referring to the west coast of Vancouver island. They may have sent some to the Pacific coast, but not to the

Supply-Fisheries
west coast of Vancouver island. I am reminded of a shipment of lobsters which was sent out to the west coast many years ago. For twenty years afterwards the argument was used that the propagation of lobsters had not proved successful, but it was proved that they had forgotten to untie the legs of the lobsters before putting them into the water. Even though nature furnishes an ideal setting, when man comes along and does a thing like that, there is only one result to be expected. We have ideal piscatorial conditions on the west coast of the island and I guarantee that if Atlantic salmon are sent out they will prove to be just as successful as they are in the state of California.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Oyster culture, $13,000.
What progress has been made wth this oyster culture?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: This work is being confined mainly to the Malpeque bay area.

I know that it is being confined to that area but I am sorry to say that the situation there is not just as we would like to see it. The fishermen feel that this vote should be spent in developing areas for public fishing, while the department seems to be of the opinion that it is better to lease these areas to private individuals for development. Did the minister not receive a petition signed by some two or three hundred fishermen protesting against the leasing of these areas?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: Protests were received.
Did the minister give any consideration to the request of the fishermen?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
The agreement was
entered into by the late government in order to establish a very large industry there. This agreement contemplated the development of the oyster industry by encouraging oyster farming on areas that would be leased for long terms so as to enable the lessees to develop their holdings. Section 5 of the agreement specifically provides that the government of Canada shal have the power of control and administration not only over the live oyster beds but over all areas that are suitable for that purpose and it expressly states that the government of Canada shall take such means as are deemed proper and advisable for the development and improvement of the growth and culture of oysters and other molluscs in the said areas. Following upon this agreement it was decided that
before encouraging anyone to go into oyster farming, the department would make an investigation to ascertain the methods by which success would be achieved. This investigation took three years and immediately thereafter the contemplated method of encouraging oyster farming was launched.

Is the minister of the opinion that the department is on the right track in leasing those areas? Does he not think he is treading on very dangerous ground? The moment he takes any public fishing area away from the public fishermen and gives it to private individuals, does he not think he is immediately courting trouble for his department and is dealing unfairly with the public fishermen?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: What the hon. member suggests has not been done by the department.
Does the minister mean to say that no public areas have been leased?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: No public producing areas have been leased.

I can hardly agree with the minister in that regard because the leasing has been done in areas where the oysters are showing signs of coming back. If those areas are not now producing in large and paying quantities, what we hoped was that with the government's cooperation with nature on the oyster areas, the beds would be brought back for public fishing. I am placed in a very difficult position in connection with this matter because a division of opinion exists and I have good friends on both sides. There are some who believe the leasing is all right and I understand they have taken out leases. There are many others who believe the oyster fisheries should be retained for the public fishermen, and any money expended should be spent with that aim in view, namely, to bring back the areas for the public fishermen. If you follow this question a little further, there are other oyster areas in the province. I see members from other counties of my province present. They have oyster areas in their counties and I do not think they would for a moment approve of the wholesale leasing of those areas. It would not be fair to them or to the fishermen of their constituencies for the department to do that.
The department may be quite honest and sincere in this matter, but I am sorry I cannot agree that the minister, through his department, is pursuing the right course in this regard. As I have stated, the moment you start handing over to private individuals the public fishing areas of any community, you are start-
Supply-Fisheries

ing trouble. I do not know what the aim of the department is; perhaps it thinks the people who take out those leases will begin to develop the areas and the Department of Fisheries will not be obliged to spend the money it otherwise would. If that is the idea, it is false economy, because it will prove a source of trouble. It has been attempted before with disastrous results to the fishing industry and we feel sure the same thing will happen again. I do not wish to emphasize this too strongly, but I might inform the minister that very largely attended indignation meetings were held in that district last summer. Those meetings were attended by as many as 500 or 600 people and committees were formed which were authorized to act on behalf of the fishermen. They protested against the leasing; they sent petitions and protests to the department and still the latter continues to lease those areas. I would like to know from the minister whether he intends to proceed with the leasing of the areas notwithstanding the fact that those protests have been received from such a large body of the fishermen.

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext:
One would
think the hcxn. member for Prince, who lives alongside this area, would give the committee a fairer picture of conditions than he has done just now. He knows very well the areas about which he speaks are not producing; that areas which are producing are not being leased by the government; that the agreement under which those areas are being leased was made about five years ago by the previous government with the then government of Prince Edward Island and that this government is only carrying out regulations contained in that agreement. I have yet to learn that the hon. member protested at that time against the agreement made by the two governments of which he was a supporter, but now he comes forward with these objections. He also speaks about meetings having been held there, which I understand were largely engineered by himself for the purpose of embarrassing the department and the government.

I have every respect for
my hon. friend, but I would ask him to withdraw that statement because it is not correct.

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext:
If my hon.
friend says that it is not correct, I shall withdraw it. The main point, however, is this: the areas to which he refers and which are being leased are not and would not be made productive, certainly not in our time, if some 
person did not lease, cultivate and make them productive. Therefore in those sections where the effort is being made it is for the good of the industry, to revive and keep alive something which would otherwise not have been revived.

Replying to the hon.
member for Kings, I did not wish to introduce a political viewpoint into this discussion. As I stated at the beginning, as many of my political friends are in favour of leasing as are against it. He refers to the agreement which was entered into by the former government. May I tell the committee frankly that under the former government and through my own instrumentality, receiving assistance from scarcely anyone but the then Minister of Fisheries, we had an appropriation placed in the estimates in order to bring back the famous Malpeque oyster. It is well known the Malpeque oyster was the most famous oyster in the world and at present oysters are being sold on the markets in various cities as Malpeque oysters although they do not come from that section at all; they come from across the border. The chairman asks why Canadian oysters are not sold in the parliamentary restaurant. The reason they are not sold is that we are not producing them in quantities sufficient to supply the market.
We did ask the Dominion government to reestablish oyster areas. Away back some fifteen or twenty years ago oyster areas were under the control of the Dominion government. At that time the local government in Prince Edward island conceived the idea that if they had the oyster areas they could lease them to private individuals, and in that way bring great revenues to the province. The local government did take over those areas and began leasing them. The result was that oysters were brought into that area indiscriminately from the southern United States, and disease became apparent on the beds, wiping out the total oyster production in that great area. The beds lay dormant a number of years. The local government had not money to expend to bring them back to production. I was particularly interested -because the area was in a district near my home. I am not ashamed to tell the committee that as a family of boys, my brothers and I made good money out of the oyster areas, and the farmers and fishermen of that community did the same thing, before the disease wiped out the industry. Then the Dominion government agreed to take over the oyster areas, and to expend money towards bringing them back to production. At this point I should like to take issue with the hon. member for

Supply-Fisheries
Kings when 'he states that those areas were taken over with the idea of leasing them, because under section 9 of the agreement there is provision that before leasing is undertaken the department at Ottawa must obtain the approval of the provincial government at Charlottetown. When the Liberal party was in power here the provincial government in Charlottetown never gave its consent to leasing, nor was any policy of leasing decided upon. If the former Minister of Fisheries were in his seat he could verify my statement, and the deputy minister can now verify it, that as a representative of the county in question, and the only one really interested in the matter, I never gave my consent to a policy of leasing. Further, leasing was never decided upon or announced as a policy of the department.
However, following a change of government in Prince Edward Island and another change here the policy of leasing was decided upon. The federal department consulted the provincial government. Advertisements for leases were inserted in newspapers and the leasing of the areas was proceeded with. The hon. member for Kings states that no public areas which were producing were leased. I ask him on what authority he makes that statement. I have been in close touch with the fishermen, and I am told that the public areas now beginning to produce are being leased. They have made similar representations to the department. Therefore before any further leases are issued I suggest very careful consideration should be given the matter. There are oyster areas in other rivers and bays. Why should Prince county be picked out and the areas leased, thereby taking away from the fishermen the public rights afforded fishermen in other counties? If there is to be one policy for one part of the province and another for another, well and good. I say however that such procedure would be quite unfair.
I do not wish to make this a political issue in any way, but I believe it is my duty in this committee to defend the rights of the public fishermen, and that the money being expended by the government should be spent in the interests of public fishermen. The hon. member for Kings states that the public areas cannot be brought back to production by the department, but that they can be brought back by private owners. I should like to know why that is so. Oysters for seed purposes can be obtained only from restricted areas where the beds show life and are now producing. The government could take the oysters off the restricted areas which
have been set aside for breeding purposes, clean the areas, and protect them properly, as well as private owners can. To say that private owners can bring back areas and that the department cannot, is begging the question, because one has as good a chance to do so as 'has the other.
The minister should give this matter his personal and careful attention; it is a matter much too serious to be trifled with. As the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough has said, one day we have one Minister of Fisheries and the next day we have another. Despite the fact that they are good men, they are busy with other work and are not giving the attention to the fishing industry that it merits. The deputy minister is doing his best, but he is nailed down to his desk, and receives very little assistance. Important matters are left to drift, and they are not given the careful consideration they should receive. I wonder if any hon. member in the house would submit to the leasing to private individuals of public fishing rights in the rivers and bays of his constituency? I venture to say there is no man in the house who would support any such policy.
No doubt I shall receive a great deal of criticism from some of my personal friends. I feel it my duty, however, to defend the rights of those public fishermen who are not here to speak for themselves.

As I understand the matter,
only nonproductive beds are being leased at the present time. I believe there has been no interference with private beds. Not one man out of fifty can make a success out of barren beds. It has been tried in my constituency; men with money have spent thousands of dollars in an endeavour to make nonproductive beds productive, and in every instance they have failed. This vote of 813,000 is for the oulture and protection of oyster beds. I believe the department is trying to do something to advance the oyster industry. The experience in the past has been 'that only those beds which have been privately owned have been successful, so far as production is concerned. In the county of Kent the Barnes Company some years ago were given a lease of certain beds, of which they have made a success. Outside of that, the beds otpen to the general public are much abused. I believe the department is 'taking steps to improve that condition, and also to improve oyster culture. I have no doubt it is endeavouring to do its best, and I suggest this small vote of $13,000 should receive the approval of the committee.
Supply-Fisheries

In my view the hon. member for Prince county has not given the committee a fair picture of the circumstances. We have been led to believe by the hon. member that the rights of public fishermen on public beds are being interfered with. This is not the case as I understand it. The public beds are very extensive in the bay referred to, and they are still available to the fishermen at large. And the Department of Fisheries has been for a number of years carrying on extensive and useful work there in clearing up the bottoms that formerly were productive but for a number of years have been non-productive by reason of that disease. The department has been sweeping, dragging, dredging and cleaning up these bottoms in the interests of the fishermen at large, and has been very successful in bringing back the fishing on those public beds. The bottom that is being leased is bottom that is not known as public fishing beds. It is non-producing, barren bottom and does not form part, as I understand it, of 'the public fishing ground of the oyster fishermen on that bay. It is being leased for the purpose of producing oysters in areas that did not produce oysters before. The former premier of Prince Edward Island, Hon. Mr. Lea, on October 26 of last year, before the maritime board of trade in the city of Charlottetown, went into this question fully. He reviewed the action that had been taken by the former government in Ottawa, and the government over which he presided as premier of Prince Edward Island; he referred to what was being done and said that it was in the best interests of the fishermen at large.
The hon. member for Prince (Mr. MacLean) says that as far as 'he is concerned he has never yet given his open consent to the leasing of these bottoms. I know the hon. member for Prince county fairly well, and sometimes 'the idea occurs to me that he is more interested in fishing for votes than in fishing for oysters.
Order.

If that is out of order I withdraw it, but it is said anyhow. The hon. member has a faculty of always withholding his consent to anything and everything, and then when the government finally takes action, if he can just get a little sympathy from some fisherman or farmer or anybody, he is quite willing to take the opposite side to that which the government has taken and try to curry favour with a few of his constituents. That has been his record in politics since I knew him first.
"Speak for yourself, John."

Never you mind. If I were the hon. member for Prince county I would be more than proud to stand up and back the Department of Fisheries for the noble efforts they are making on behalf of his constituents and his county to restore that important industry, and I would do anything and everything I could to strengthen the hands of the department. I will say that if the hon. member does not appreciate that $13,000 that we are voting, that is being spent almost entirely in Prince county, then we will make a recommendation to the Department of Fisheries that for the time being we give Prince county the go-by, for we are mighty willing to spend it in Kings and Queens.

I think my good friend from Queens is measuring other people's corn in bis own half bushel. I am not quite as smooth as my hon. friend is and not so able to fish for votes as he is. I wish to tell my hon. friend in the first place that we are not objecting to the spending of this money.
What are you objecting to?
We are objecting to the leasing of the areas. My good friend is an inland farmer, and I would tell him to stick to his potatoes and leave things alone that he doesn't know about.
I do not know that you are much of a fisherman.

My hon. friend is not entitled to talk about the oyster industry in the county of Prince. He is a good-natured gentleman from an inland district, and we must pardon him if he has not a full grasp of the situation as it appears to us who are right on the ground and know. The difficulty is that these areas are being leased to people, whose farms front on the rivers and bays. Naturally the oysters are coming back in the heads of the rivers and bays, in shallow water near the shore. The deputy minister knows perfectly well that where the areas are being taken is not out in the big bays and rivers but along the shore fronts of the different people who reside along these fronts. These are ithe places where, the fishermen tell me, the oysters are coming back. Nothing would please me better than if under this private ownership a great industry could be built up, but my hon. friend from Queens knows very well that it was attempted before, and he knows that an industry that was worth millions of dollars to the province of Prince Edward Island was wiped out of existence

Supply-Fisheries
through that policy. Why should we go blindly into the same trap again, just when the disease has run its course? Scientists told us at the time that this disease had been introduced from some unknown source and that it would likely run its course in seven or eight or ten years. They were right in that, because after ft had killed out everything in the way of shellfish in those bays and rivers the oysters began to come back, and, as I have said, they are coming back at the heads of the rivers and bays. There is no one more interested in this than I am; I am willing to accept any good, constructive suggestions, but I do not want to be classed as one who is endeavouring to do an injury to the oyster industry or anyone interested in it. What I want is to bring the oyster industry back for the public fisherman, and I do not think that once the whole shore area right around the rivers and bays is leased there will be much chance for the public oyster fisherman to make a living.
I am not going to labour this any further; I leave it with the Acting Minister of Fisheries and his deputy. I think that in the interests of all concerned no more leases should be granted until the matter is looked into thoroughly. I would invite my hon. friend from Queens to come up there and meet the fishermen. I would invite him and his colleagues and the hon. member for Kings to go out there on the patrol boat and see the areas that have been leased, see the work that has been carried on, and if they will just give the word there will be a meeting called that will be attended by thousands of people so that they can get the viewpoint of the fishermen right on the ground.

I do not wish to prolong the debate on this question. My hon. friend thinks that I do not know an oyster from a potato. That is hardly true. I happened to be a member of the local government in Prince Edward Island from 1912 to 1916 when the oyster areas were taken over from the federal government by the provincial government. They were taken over at that time for the express purpose of attempting to plant oysters on what was then barren bottom. At that time the active beds were producing oysteTs in great quantities and they were not interfered with in any way. In order to plant these bottoms and build up the industry, areas that were known to be barren were leased to fishermen mostly, and men who are known as farmer-fishermen-men who engage in both occupations-who are adjacent to the areas leased. For some reason or other small seed oysters were imported from the state of 53719-267
Rhode Island and planted on these barren bottoms. Shortly after that some disease visited these oyster beds. Some of the scientists-I do not know whether or not they are very great scientists-blamed that disease upon the imported oysters from Rhode Island, but I am not able to subscribe to that theory, though. I am not a scientist, I am a plain, ordinary inlander, as my hon. friend from Prince calls me, though my farm does touch the Northumberland straits. To my mind this is the question: If the disease was imported with those seed oysters from Rhode Island why were there any live oysters left there; why were they not dead of the disease before we brought them here? I want to tell the committee that around the shores of Prince Edward Island we have mussel mud beds from which we farmers dig mussel mud for fertilizer. These beds are known to be sixty feet deep in places, and to my mind that proves that these periodical waves of disease or epidemics have been going on since Adam went into long pants, and will continue as long as the sun rises and sets.
So I could never subscribe to the theory that the disease was imported from Rhode Island or anywhere else. It did happen, however, that a very valuable type of oyster, the Malpeque oyster, was wiped out, and we all regret that very much. Let me say, however-and I have this information from the Department of Fisheries-that all the oysters did not die; apparently some were immune to the disease and survived the epidemic. These are now restocking the beds, with the aid that is being given by the Department of Fisheries. It is the same old story; I am not a medical man, but I have been told that if a wave or epidemic of typhoid or diphtheria sweeps through a settlement people here and there will not contract that disease; apparently they are immune to it. This seems to have been the case with the oysters; a few survived the storm, and these beds are being restocked by these surviving oysters. As I said before the Department of Fisheries is making every effort, in aid of the fishermen at large, to restock the public beds, but it is the barren bottoms that are being leased to these fishermen and farmer fishermen in order to rebuild a great industry in Prince county.

Thank you. Just before we leave this vote I should 'like to refer to something I probably should have mentioned in connection with item 163. I notice that the department, with laudable enterprise, has been holding classes for the fishermen of the Atlantic coast. They have been attended by some thirty-five men and are appreciated so much that this year there was quite a rush to join. Many more fishermen applied for enrolment than could be admitted, and they had to limit the number. These fishermen's courses include instruction in such subjects as the preparation of dried, boneless and pickled fish, the coopering of barrels, navigation, motor engines and refrigeration, and there is also elementary instruction in chemistry, bacteriology and biology. I applied for our share of this, but I was told that the biological board did not think it was necessary, which was a very nice compliment since it implied at least that on the Pacific we did not need instruction. While I am proud to accept that compliment on behalf of our fishermen there, I do not think the men themselves would admit that they were beyond instruction or the need of information. I do submit that, if they do not receive anything out of that $160,000 grant made in the other vote, they might at least be given a share of this instructional vote. We are told that the fishermen on the Pacific coast do not want to learn anything about pickling cod. Quite so, but we want to know about pickling and smoking herring; we want to know how to put up to the best advantage the various fish we catch. Our fishermen would also appreciate some information in connection with motor engines, and some elementary instruction in

Supply-Fisheries
the other subjects mentioned. I cannot see that the discrimination can be justified by putting us off with some compliment to the effect that we are so advanced as not to need instruction. That is not so. I do submit that these classes should be inaugurated on the Pacific coast as well as on the Atlantic. Our friend from Antigonish-Guysborough tells us that we were not in existence at one time so far as the fishing industry is concerned, that we are amateurs, that we have just come into the business. Well, isn't that all the more reason for our getting some instruction? Certainly. I submit that the fishermen on the Pacific coast, particularly those who are newcomers to the trade, should be encouraged to make the best of their facilities. The minister is taking steps to see that this is done on the Atlantic and it is unfair not to do the same thing on the Pacific.

I do not quite understand the point of view of the hon. gentleman. If he would ask the department to increase the vote so that a certain amount might be spent in British Columbia I could see the force of his remarks. But he is trying to take the money voted for work on the Atlantic coast.
No.

He tried to get part of the $160,000 which the American government paid this country for purposes distinctly applicable to the maritimes, and now he objects to a vote of $4,500 to provide, subject to the approval of the governor in council, a grant to maritime fishermen. The difference between myself, representing a constituency in one of the Atlantic provinces, and the hon. gentleman from Comox-Alberni, is quite apparent. If you will glance at the estimates you will see that just before this $4,500 item was called we passed without discussion or criticism from maritime members a vote of $29,500 entirely for Pacific coast fisheries. We do not object to this government spending money on the Pacific coast; whatever is necessary for the development or the protection of the fisheries there, we as members from the maritime provinces will vote for it. But when the department thinks that it is in the interests of the fishermen that a small amount of $4,500 should be voted to encourage fishermen in the maritime provinces, it ill becomes the hon. member for Comox-Alberni to object. We are passing tens of thousands of dollars in the interests of British Columbia fishermen and I do not think he should object to a vote for the maritimes.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Salaries and disbursements of fishery officers and guardians, fisheries patrol and fisheries protection services, $1,022,000.

I have already protested against an order in council passed on March 10 last allowing purse seine fishing at the mouth of the Fraser river, and I want now to reiterate that protest. First of all I wish to direct the attention of the minister to the fact that the committee on fisheries is not being given anything to do. The committee is struck every year and the names of the members are printed; yet important matters are put through by order in council without the committee on fisheries being given an opportunity to discuss them. This is all the more serious when we remember that this prder in council was passed while the house was sitting. It may be argued that it is necessary to pass certain orders in council when the house is not in session, but I think it is something to be taken serious note of that when the house is in session matters affecting an industry should be put through without any reference whatever to the committee. When the house is sitting matters affecting any industry should go before the particular committee concerned. When the Minister of Agriculture had certain matters under consideration with regard to
Supply-Fisheries

agriculture ihe referred them to the committee, and we should be treated in like manner with respect to the fisheries.
I wrote to the minister on February 8, protesting against the order in council I am now discussing, and I received an answer on the tenth. I wish to take issue with some of the statements made in that letter. For instance, it was said therein that the question would receive consideration, though as a matter of fact, at the time this letter was sent out, the order in council I believe had been passed. I do not think that is a fair way to treat any member especially when he writes protesting against something that affects twelve or fifteen hundred fishermen. At 'least it should have been pointed out that the order in council had been passed. I received the letter on the tenth saying that the matter would be given consideration, but as a matter of fact it had been put through by order in council and was later published in the Gazette. The letter also states that if these advanced fish could be caught before the Fraser river is reached their full value for canning would be safeguarded. I am informed that these salmon are caught by the average gill netter before they reach fresh water. For the information of the committee I would point out that one seine boat will do away with perhaps twenty or thirty individual fishermen. In these days when we are endeavouring to find work for the unemployed, and when that is almost impossible, I do not think that seines should be allowed to operate right in the mouth of the Fraser river and up to tine international boundary. The average seine boat carries a net about twelve hundred feet long and eighty' feet deep. It forms a sort of purse. They make a circle and the bottom is drawn, and they will pick up anything from one thousand to five thousand fish at a time. Another of the disastrous results of the operations of these seine boats is the fact that they break up the schools of fish. The fish previous to entering the Fraser river are in schools made up of thousands and thousands of fish and if these seine boats are allowed to swirl in with their purse sines they will break them up. It takes some time before the schools gather together again before making their way up the Fraser river to spawn. These seine boats will also catch some late-run sockeye. I have it on the authority of fishermen who are conversant with the river that the seine boats will catch two pink salmon to one sockeye. While it is intended that these boats will catch only pink salmon, the fact is that considerable sockeye will be caught as well. Protests have been made to the minister and to the department and indignation meetings have been held
CMr Reid.]
against this order in council. I have received many letters from individual fishermen, and I would like to quote one as follows:
If they are allowed to use seines at the mouth of the river, it is goodbye fish on the Fraser. They are the most destructive means of fishing; they are floating traps, etc.
That is also the contention which was put forward when the deputy minister held his meeting in New Westminster. It is very unfortunate that this action should be taken at a time when a bill to do away with traps at the international boundary was being introduced into the legislature of Washington state. I have a newspaper report reading as follows:
Abolition of Fish Traps is Proposed in Washington
Olympia, Wash., Feb. 13.-Abolition of fish traps and seine nets in Washington waters, was asked to-day in a house bill introduced by Hugh Herrin of Pierre county. Seine and drag nets, fish traps and wheels would be prohibited in rivers and lakes, and in all Washington waters when used commercially, the bill provided.
It was very unfortunate that this order in council should have been passed at a time when a bill to abolish traps was being presented before the Washington state legislature. Seine traps are used in the state of Washington close to the international boundary and the argument is put forward that we should also allow the use of seines. Several canneries have also always advocated the use of traps. As I say, it is most unfortunate that this action should have been taken just at a time we were trying to get through a sockeye salmon treaty and when a bill was being introduced in Washington state to do away with traps and seines. Between 1,200 and 1,500 fishermen will be thrown out of employment if this order in council is continued in force. I appeal to 'the minister to cancel it right away. I know the argument will be used that we are after quality fish, that we want to be able to command the best markets in Great Britain, but if the minister will look up the figure he will find that the great percentage of the catch of pinks is not made in the Fraser river. The last time this matter was before the committee I sent a map across to the minister which showed that the seines which are being allowed to operate in the Fraser river would operate in shallow water. Under this order in council, the seiners will be permitted to fish where individual gill netters now operate. I have been over this area oftener than even the deputy minister and I know that the gill netters use the shallow waters and the waters of the gulf. If the seine boats are permitted to enter this area, the individual fishermen

Supply-Fisheries
might just as well give up business entirely.
I again repeat that this matter should have been referred to the fisheries committee so that full discussion could have been had in connection with the whole matter. More than fifteen hundred individuals will be affected and most of these fishermen are heads of families. The danger is that once these seine boats are allowed to operate, the cry will go up for the use of traps. The seine boats are practically floating traps and no gill net boat will be able to operate. These seine boats are powered and carry a crew of from four to seven. They use nets twelve hundred feet in length which form a purse eighty feet deep. When they get into a school of fish, they lift up the net and I have heard of instances where they have brought up from seven to eight thousand fish in one lift. Trouble is also caused by the breaking up of the schools. Once they are broken up it takes days for them to collect together again before making their way up the river to spawn. I ask the minister in all seriousness to reconsider this matter and have the order in council rescinded. When the matter was up before I asked him to send it to a committee and he said at that time he would consider my suggestion, but nothing further was done.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
The day the letter
was sent to my hon. friend this matter came up before the cabinet. It was considered from every angle and the cabinet finally came to the conclusion that the regulation should be adopted. The experts claim that this will not affect the fishermen of the Fraser river. The first reason is that when the fish come up the Fraser river they are not in good condition and would not be accepted to-day on the market. The second reason is that seining is restricted to an area largely south of the Fraser river waters in which practically no gill netting is conducted. The third reason is that the seine fishing is also restricted by the regulations to the period when the pink salmon and late run sockeye are moving in large quantities, that is from August 25 to September 30, and providing that in years when there is a large run of late sockeye, fishing may go on until the end of October. Fishing by gill netters will not be interfered with. They may fish as heretofore, but as previously pointed out, after the pink salmon or late-run sockeye reach the Fraser, very few of the fish taken will meet present canning requirements, and to the extent that the gill netters fish out in the gulf of Georgia, the catch will be as marketable as in the past. Hence, if seining were not allowed, the run of pinks and late sockeyes which are heavily
fished in the United States would have to be permitted to supply largely our requirements on the Canadian side. It is estimated that a canned product having a value of from $500,000 to $1,000,000 is involved. The pack of pink salmon in the Fraser river and Puget sound for the past four years is as follows:
