This shows that the larger fishing is done at Puget sound. After our experts' explanation, we came to the conclusion that this regulation should be adopted and we are making a trial. We shall see how it works for a year and if it is advisable later on to amend the regulation, this will be done.

But the department this year is departing from its oft-repeated policy which was to keep the seines down to as few as possible.
As regards the letter that I received on the tenth, it said that the department was considering the question. My complaint was that while I was told so in that letter, as a matter of fact the order in council had already been passed and I was not informed in the letter that the order in council had been passed. I should like to know who asked that seining be allowed in the gulf. If seining had been allowed close to the international boundary, it would have been bad enough, but not as bad as it is at present. If the minister will examine the map of which I sent him a copy and look at the area covered by the order in council, he will see that it practically blocks off the mouth of the Fraser river, and right to the waters where the gill net boats operate. It may be true, as he says, the Puget sound pack is high as compared with the Fraser river pack, but I would point out that the pack of pink salmon in the Fraser river was comparatively small as compared with the pack of pink salmon over the rest of British Columbia. The salmon caught further north in the Skeena and Naas rivers is caught in salt water and is I believe first-class fish and the pack in proportion to that of the Fraser river is very large. Why should the fishermen who are involved not be considered? I have here a letter from an association dealing with these conditions, part of which states:
Under the circumstances why the department should even consider changing its oft repeated policy of eliminating seines wherever possible and permitting gill netting so as to employ more men in the industry is a puzzle
Supply-Fisheries

to fishermen, for more than ever before should the stated policy now be adhered to. Seines, merely mobile, floating traps, "ride" the schools of salmon to utter extinction, while gill nets allow a good escapement to seed the spawning beds.
I do not know whether a copy of tha-t was sent to the minister, 'but it is sent to me by the British Columbia Protective Fishermen's Association.
Another letter states:
Unfortunately, however, your letter arrived this morning and in this evening's Province is an item under Ottawa date saying that seining has been granted in the Gulf of Georgia during the period between August 25 and September 30 in odd-numbered years and between September 1 and September 30 in even-numbered years. Also they may seine for sockeye during the "big run" of late fish until October 31.
This simply means farewell to the medium and late runs of sockeye-
The fishermen say that not only will the seines catch pinks but the late-run sockeye "will be interfered with.
-so far as the Fraser river fishermen are concerned. There are always sockeye mixed up with pinks, or humpbacks, as the fishermen call them, and the ratio is often three pinks to one sockeye.
It certainly is disheartening to see such a fine bunch of settlers on the Fraser river, who are manfully struggling to keep off the relief lists, sacrificed for the canners and seine boat owners-
-who, I believe, are the ones who asked that seining be allowed in the gulf of Georgia. I believe the minister as well as his deputy know the fishermen have long protested the use of seines. When the deputy minister was out on the coast last fall he attended three, if not four meetings and at two at least vigorous protests by the fishermen were made against seining. Why the department has now departed from its oft-repeated policy is something the fishermen and the rest of us cannot understand. In spite of all the minister says, I believe the order in council should not be put into effect; it should be rescinded, especially in times such as we are going through when it is impossible for men to obtain any kind of job. This is going to affect 1,200 or 1,500 fishermen. Surely the minister will agree with me that the men who are in the business, who have fishing boats, Should know something about the matter and should reoeive first consideration. I ask the minister seriously: W'ho requested this and why could the matter not have been placed before the committee on fisheries? Why was that committee appointed, if not to discuss matters of this kind? Those are two pertinent questions I should like to ask the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: The request for that regulation was made by the United Fishermen's Association composed of over 1,000 fishermen, and also by all the canners in , order to increase business, because they contended that those fish when caught up the Fraser river were no good for the market and this was a loss to the fishermen and to the canners. There was no objection on the part of the Fraser river canners.
The canners.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: Yes.

Is it not a fact that the
United Fishermen's Association is composed mostly of seine boat owners?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: Some; not all.
Naturally they would advocate this. The fact that seine boat owners urge more latitude in seining is hardly an argument.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
But the government
has to look after the interests of all the fishermen.
There are 1,500 fishermen involved in this, who are protesting against the use of seines.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: But it was represented and proof was put before the government that it did not affeot the 1,200 fishermen of whom my non. friend speaks, because those are salt water fish and when they are up the Fraser river, they are of no value to the market and are a loss.
Proof was placed before the deputy at the meeting held in New Westminster. Protestations were made before a full meeting; they have always protested seining in that gulf.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: The hon. member has askedl why there was no meeting of the fisheries committee to study that regulation. Does the hon. member suggest that before any regulation is adopted it should go before that committee, and that we should wait until the house and committee are sitting before passing any regulations? The act gives power to the governor in council to pass regulations, and that power was exercised.

To be fair, the minister should have added that the house was sitting at the time. We were here in the month of February when the order in council was passed. This is a matter of great importance, affecting 1,500 people. Protests were received by the minister and by many members of parliament, and it is of some importance. The minister

Supply-Fisheries
should have referred the matter to the fisheries committee. Earlier in my remarks I pointed out that had the house not been in session there may have been some excuse for enforcing some minor regulation, but when we were in session a matter of such importance as this should have gone before that committee for discussion and consideration. In regard to the inspection of hay and straw the Minister of Agriculture was good enough to move that the matter be referred to the agriculture committee. The Acting Minister of Fisheries asks: Would you have referred this matter to a committee? My answer is that I certainly would have, and why not when the house was sitting?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: I ask the hon. member not to be so insistent; let us have a trial for a year, so that we may see what will happen. There is a difference of opinion among the citizens of the Pacific coast; some share my ihon. friend's views, and others are of a different opinion, namely that the regulation does not affect the fishermen of the Fraser river. Let us try out the regulation, and if later on it is felt that it is not favourable, and that the injury done to the fishermen of the north Fraser river is greater than the benefit received by other fishermen, the regulation can be changed. Let us try it out for a year.

I have not expressed merely
my own opinion, but that also of the British Columbia Fishermen's Protective Association. Their statement is to the effect that the regulation is certainly detrimental, and that it means good-bye to fishing on the Fraser river. There will be practically a trap in the mouth of the Fraser river. As I have pointed out, this regulation is but the thin end of the wedge. Cannery interests, and others, have advocated that we put traps along the international boundary, and use seines, as the Americans are doing. Our effort has been towards conservation of the fish, and if possible to get the Americans to stop trapping and seining. It so happens that this year a bill was presented in the legislature of the state of Washington asking for the abolition of traps and seines on the American side. In the debate on that bill I understand it was stated that Canada did not use traps or seines. Now, however, they will be able to say, "Well, Canada is using seines, and so we will continue their use."
I still press that the regulation should be held up. The British Columbia Fishermen's Protective Association did not make merely a wild guess when they stated that 1,500 fishermen would be affected.

Of course it goes without
saying that seiners would be in favour of the regulation. After an argument has been advanced against a certain policy it seems to me that the suggestion to let the matter rest for a year is a very poor one. It is not always well to do that. Sometimes irreparable damage is done in a year's time, and to say that the Fraser river fishermen will not be harmed is a burlesque on the facts.
There is one point I should like to add to those mentioned by the hon. member for New Westminster. The minister has stated that through the use of seines the fish will be fresher when caught. As to the habits of these fish, they are out in the open ocean, on their own; that is, they are not associated with other fish. As they draw nearer fresh water they do not go.straight up the river, but hang around. I do not know whether or not some biological condition is responsible for their actions; I am simply stating what they do, not why they do it., After playing around for some time, they bunch; that is the time for which the seiner is waiting. He does not take them when they are loose, because that would not pay. The placing of the seine is an expensive and long operation, The seiner waits until the fish school; they are schooling about the time they are ready to go up the river. Sometimes they hang around for weeks. The gill netter can afford to catch them before they school. They gc in and out ahead of the seiners, catching the fish when they are separated, and are certainly of better quality. In a year when there was a heavy run of water probably the fish would not linger, but in a dry season they linger a great deal. Fish caught in .the gill nets would be probably of a better quality, because they are caught at an earlier period. It is a well known fact that it does not pay the seiner to set for fish which are not more or less schooled or bunched together.
The minister suggests that we should try the regulation for a year. Fishermen on the Fraser river have been operating for over thirty years. It is now proposed in these days of unemployment and distress to do something which certainly will affect their livelihood. The business would be placed in the hands of a few seine boats employing half a dozen men each. Every seine boat would put at least twenty gill netters out of occupation. It will put them out of other fishing, because this is only a sort of fill in. If they lose at that time they are liable to lose their livelihood altogether.
I wish now to revert to the notorious order in council No. 206 passed on February 3,
Supply-Fisheries

providing that salmon could not be inspected and get a certificate unless they had been landed on the wharf where they were canned within twenty-four hours after being caught, unless being gutted and iced. On April 4, I brought the matter to the attention of the minister, stating that the British Columbia legislature had unanimously passed a resolution against this order in council. Upon that occasion I asked him what he purposed doing. His reply was that he would check up on the accuracy of the report-a poor compliment to me-and then would take the matter into very serious consideration.
From the votes and proceedings of March 29, of the legislative assembly of the province of British Columbia I read the following:
Half-past eight o'clock p.m.
The house resumed the adjourned debate on the motion moved by Mr. Loutet on March 21-
Eight days before.
-as follows:
That this legislature goes on record as being emphatically opposed to the order in council P.C. 206 passed on February 3, 1933, by the government of Canada, regarding the delivery of salmon at a cannery within twenty-four hours after being caught.
The debate continued.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Motion agreed to.
A week elapsed between the introduction of the motion and its adoption. Further debate ensued after which the motion was unanimously agreed to. In the light of the information which he has received I ask the minister now what his decision is. The document I have read is authentic; can the minister tell me Whether or not he will revise his opinion, or what his decision will be?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine

speechtext:
I do not think the chances of ever receiving a reply are good. The government of British Columbia is in a state of flux at present, liable to dissolve into its constituent molecules at any moment. If on the fourth of April the minister was advised, as he was, it would not have taken him long to send a wire to the premier or provincial secretary asking about the passing of this resolution, which was passed on March 29.
I think it was up to the minister to carry out his pledge that he was going to check it up, before now. Here at least it is the actual official report, the votes and proceedings of British Columbia. That has been in my possession for weeks; the motion was passed 
on the 29th of March, nearly a month ago. The session is wearing to its end; this is the last occasion to debate it, and still he says 'he is waiting for the premier of British Columbia to get around to expressing an opinion. What opinion does he need? The legislature passed it; fifty premiers cannot gainsay that. He did not oppose it; he had a huge majority, and we must presume that that is the reasoned decision of the legislature of British Columbia. I am sorry the minister has not got a definite statement; I must assume, I suppose, that he does not intend to change his decision.
I want to take this opportunity, while protesting against the lack of action, to refer to a meeting of the board of trade in Vancouver a few days ago. The record of it appears in the newspaper in big headlines three-eighths of an inch high, reading:
Reds blamed by Salmon Canners.
Objection to Twenty-four Hour Packing Order Charged to Communists.
It is popular nowadays to charge everything to the communists. I think we as public men ought to give a lead and cut out this nonsense
Hear, hear.

-that everyone who disagrees with us is a red or a bolshevik. The bolshevik phase is passing; we now call them reds. Here is a whole column of the views of a Mr. Richard Bell-Irving addressing the board of trade on that occasion. That was on the front page. What about the other side of the picture? Here is the other side, a little paragraph three inches long on the back page of a subsequent issue, and small headlines: "Denies Communists Prompted Protest. A man named Johnson, an executive of the fishermen's organization, says his organization is not communistic; it is affiliated with the trades and labour council; its membership consists of 1,200 fishermen of whom 300 are returned soldiers. Communistic principles are not entertained, and the body is merely endeavouring to improve fishing conditions." But that appeared on the back page in small print. The popular idea goes out to the world, or to British Columbia, that the fishermen have been caught with the reds behind them spreading this propaganda.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: Do I understand that the Vancouver board of trade approved of the regulations?

I would give them credit for more sense. This was an address given by Mr. Bell-Irving, and it is not on record that

Supply-Fisheries
any action was taken. He was speaking at a luncheon of the foreign trade bureau of the board. As to whether the board of trade of Vancouver ever took any official action, they may have, but I do not know.
I quote again from this article:
Objections . . . were inspired by printed handbills distributed early in March by communists. The measure meets with approval of all "practical fishermen."
In those few words there are two deliberate falsehoods. The measure is not approved by all practical fishermen, and the objections to it were not inspired by printed hand bills distributed by communists early in March. I spoke in this house on the 21st of February, so the communists could not have inspired it by handbills early in March.
There was a reference in that same address of Mr. Bell-Irving to myself-a somewhat slimy reference; I will not bother the house denying it. It did not appear in the press; but it was taken down in writing, and he will be given an opportunity either to prove or to retract the statement. But I will not take the time of the house with my private troubles.
Then we come to another quotation about this meeting:
Objections to the new regulations, Mr. Bell-Irving charged, did not come to the surface for a week or ten days, and were "inspired" by a few small operators whose single-cannery operations might be affected.
Note that. The regulations were printed in the Gazette of February IS-that was a Saturday-and I spoke on the subject the following Tuesday, the very first opportunity that presented itself; the statement that it did not come to the surface for a week or ten days is nonsense. He may have had privy knowledge of it before that, I do not deny it; because he was the instigator of the whole movement, but the general p-ublic knew nothing until the regulations were gazetted on the 18th of February. Then he says it is "inspired by a few small operators." It was said before to have been inspired by the reds, but now, in the same column, it is inspired "by a few small operators whose single cannery operations might be affected." Is there anything wrong in having a single cannery? Is the right of way in legislation and policy to be given only to those who control a dozen canneries? There is nothing improper about being only a single cannery operator; he has a perfect right to express his sentiment. It is rather funny, if he is an operator, that the operators should not all think alike in the matter, if it is as Mr. Bell-Irving says.
Then we find that Mr. Bell-Irving made a vigorous defence of the regulations providing that canned salmon can be given first grade certificates only if canned within twenty-four hours after the catch. That is a total misstatement; that is not the regulation, and no one knows it better than Mr. Bell-Irving. If it were that it would have quite a different aspect. The regulation is that it be landed at the cannery, where it is going to be canned heaven knows when, within twenty-four hours after being caught-a different proposition altogether. I have a letter in my possession from a cannery man who says he has known the fish to have been brought in in the evening and left on that hot floor-and it is a hot floor in the summer time in these little inlets where the sun beats down on a tin roof-from one evening until the following afternoon. Is that provided against in the regulations? No; it is only to compel them to bring it to the cannery wharf within twenty-four hours. That shows the insincerity of the thing.
Now let us go back to the reasons alleged for the objections made. Two contrary reasons are given-one that it is inspired by the reds, and the other that it is inspired by the single cannery owners. And they are classed both together as being unworthy of credit. What about the city councils? Why did three city councils unanimously pass a resolution against this order in council? And one was the city of Victoria, not noted to be red in its colouring. Boards of trade all over the lower province passed resolutions against it. Then we find a resolution introduced in the local house by Mr. Loufet, the alble Conservative member for North Vancouver. Would you call him a red? We in British Columbia do not so regard him. Then again, what about passing it through the legislature? Are they red? They consist, if my memory is correct, of 48 members, 36 of whom are Conservative, 11 Liberal and 1 Labour. It is hardly a place one would expect to find red propaganda very successful. But the reds put it all over the legislature of British Columbia, it is suggested, and the other side was invited and expressed its views; the cannery men had a delegation. But the reds put it all over the legislature, or was it the men with the single cannery that did it? It is funny how it was unanimous.
But let me tell the minister this is the way to make reds. He says the reds distributed handbills. I know nothing of that. They may have done so; they may have taken advantage of the facts, but who brought the facts into existence? They may have taken advantage
Supply-Fisheries

of the gross injustice perpetrated by order in council 206 to arouse and stimulate discontent. That is their job and their policy, though I think it is a poor one. They may have done that, but the blame must lie at the door of those who passed the legislation which made it possible for a red to appeal to the sense of injustice aroused among the fishermen and the single cannery owners. This question was not discussed at the meetings attended by the deputy minister; it was not discussed in our fisheries committee; it was put through by political pull. I do not hesitate at all to make that statement.
Let me outline what happened. There are three large cannery companies who claim to represent ninety per cent of the output of canned salmon in British Columbia. I do not for a moment certify to that statement in the light of the contradictions to which I have already referred, but certainly they do represent a large portion of the canning industry of British Columbia. They were out, as they have been for many years, to stop competition in canning and in buying salmon. That is their purpose, and this is the latest method they have adopted to put through their policy. Unfortunately I happen to hold some bonds of one of those companies, so I may be held to be disinterested when opposing them, but I doubt very much whether even from the point of view of the canneries themselves this is a wise policy; in fact I am sure it is not. My idea of the way to promote success in any industry, canning or anything else, is to have shrewd and careful management and very close cooperation with customers and employees, and those with whom you have to deal. That is not the way these cannery owners are going about it; they are trying to create depression, distress and ill-will among the fishermen whose cooperation is of the greatest value to them. Therefore I say I do not think this is a good policy even from their point of view; certainly they should not go about trying to put their competitors out of business by political means.
At any rate they decided to try to put this over. They did not say anything at the meetings called for that purpose in British Columbia, to which they were especially invited and which were attended by the deputy minister or the minister himself. Not a word was said about it imtil after the minister had gone home and peace had descended. We thought we knew the worst that could happen to us, but then a delegation came to Ottawa. On January 20 the department went on record that they did not know anything about the
	.
matter. I heard some rumours about it and I wrote the department, who replied that there was nothing of the kind contemplated or had been brought to the attention of the department. Then on February 3 the whole thing was cut and dried and the order in council signed. All hon. gentlemen know that it takes quite a while to get an order in council signed after it has been prepared, so it is easy to imagine the rush with which this was put through. My letter was dated January 20, and I do not know what interval elapsed after that before the order in council was prepared, but certainly it was put through in a very short time.
The other day the suggestion was made that this was not going to work out in the way I predicted, that it would not do away with competition in buying from the fishermen. We were told that there were lots of canneries, that there were ten or fifteen in every distriot. There are thirty-six subdistricts in British Columbia-I counted them the other day-and last year there were thirty-five canneries operating. In previous years there have been as many as seventy-five, but last year there were only thirty-five. Some of these subdistricts may not have a cannery at all while others may have two, but I know of no subdistriot in my territory that has more than two. You know how easy it is for two competitors to get together and make an arrangement.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
But there are only three
districts.
There are only three districts having supervisors, but they are so big that you could not carry out this plan within their borders.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
That was the reference
to the number of canneries in a district, not what my hon. friend is seeking to suggest now.

I was referring to the Minister of Trade and Commerce, who said they were divided into subdistricts, and I was quoting the subdistricts. The three large districts about which the minister speaks now are so large that you could not carry out this twenty-four hour rule in any but district No. 1. Speaking on another subject, and indeed referring to this matter, the minister asked the other day why we should not try this out for a year, and then change it if it did not work out well. These identical words were used last year, Mr. Chairman, when the government introduced their system for the inspection of canned salmon. I took exception, not to the principle, which was

Supply-F isheries
admirable, but to the method, which I said was entirely unsatisfactory and would prove unworkable. The argument advanced then was, "Try it for a year, anyway, and see how it works." We did not need to wait for a year; it proved so utterly ineffective that it had to be changed on three different occasions, so that finally the regulations occupied five and a half times their original space. I am not going into that just now except to say that I am going to take the minister at his word. Speaking of these inspection regulations in April last the minister said, "Well, try it for a year." We did not even try it for a year. The regulations did not come into effect until June 1, and they could not possibly apply to the inspection of canned salmon until a couple of months later. On February 3, however, five months later, it was suddenly found that they were all wrong, [DOT]that they were all wet, although they had been changed three times. It was found necessary to change not a clause or a detail of administration but the whole system. I have here a quotation from a Conservative newspaper in British Columbia, no doubt inspired by the cannery interests. Here they make a report on this inspection; they say that the system became operative last June, and only about a little over one per cent were found unfit for the certificate. That is a fine record. There were 968,500 cases of salmon examined, and 1-2 per cent were found unqualified for the first certificate. That looks as though the pack had been pretty good, doesn't it?
The figures testify plainly-
This is not my opinion; this is the cannery-inspired information appearing in the press.
-to the quality of the salmon which go into the cans in British Columbia and to the efficiency and care which is used in the cannery operations, for members of the inspection board are experts of long experience and established reputation in the salmon trade, and canned salmon, which they find worthy of certification must be of unquestionable quality.
I suppose that was not intended to help put over this twenty-four hour deal. Then the picture changed suddenly; between January 20 and February 3 it was found necessary not to amend the regulations but to upset them altogether. Previously these highly qualified men looked at the salmon and their duty, according to their instructions, was to pass it if it was good and to condemn it if it was bad. What is the position with this newfangled idea? If it is bad they can condemn it but if it is good they cannot pass it. It may be as good as any salmon they ever saw in cans, but they cannot pass it unless they get some proof that the salmon were landed
at the wharf where they were afterwards canned within twenty-four hours after being caught. How can they find that out? A cannery man may pack 60,000 or 70,000 cases; he may have two or three canneries. His pack will be assembled in Vancouver, since that is the shipping point, and he may have
10,000	or 20,000 cases inspected. The inspector may find the salmon quite all right; it may be firm, well packed and complying with the law in every respect, but he cannot give a certificate until he has proof that it was landed on the wharf within twenty-four hours after being caught. How can he get that proof? I directed that question to the department, and months after the regulation was in force I was told that the matter was still under consideration. Is the cannery man to give the certificate? Is he to take an oath about something in regard to which he cannot be informed? Is some agent to do it? Who is to take the oath? And if it is not an oath it is a joke. The cannery man can say, "I saw a fisherman come to my wharf with some fish, but I do not know how long they had been caught. He told me they had been caught so many hours but I did not swear him. To the best of my knowledge and belief they were caught within twenty-four hours of being landed." That is what he is likely to say, and he would be a fool if he did not say so. But without the expenditure of an enormous amount of money and having an inspector at every cannery it will be impossible to find out whether the fish had been caught within twenty-four hours or not. This declaration will be a blot on the record of the department, which during the last ten years has been trying to cooperate with the cannery men on the one hand and with the fishermen on the other. Nothing should be passed here unless it has been first discussed at meetings at which all parties interested can be represented. In the past the meetings of the deputy minister were open to everyone, cannery men, fishermen and the public. Everyone was welcome and anything that could not be discussed was regarded with suspicion. This declaration, I repeat, will remain a blot on the record of the department until it is removed. Before I sit down I want to ask this question. Has the department, or have the officers, so far developed or conceived any system by which it can be proved to the inspectors that fish have been caught as required within twenty-four hours of being landed at the wharf.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
Our inspectors obtain from the canners a sworn declaration to the effect; they have to ascertain that the fish have been taken within twenty-four hours of
Supply-Fisheries

being landed at the cannery. We are following a regulation similar to one which is in force in Scotland and is working quite satisfactorily there. I am afraid that my hon. friend did not understand me the other day when I told the house that I would await official confirmation of the resolution adopted by the house in British Columbia. I never questioned my hon. friend's statements, but I think it was fair for the government to await the confirmation of that resolution. I do not think however that even if that resolution were adopted it would alter the decision of the government in this matter. In my opinion my hon. friend, instead of helping the fishermen of the western coast, is injuring their business by his insistence in this regard. Our officials so far are of the opinion that the regulation adopted last year and reinforced by the one adopted this year will have the effect of enhancing the price of fish rather than reducing it.
Who says that?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
Our officials. As a
matter of fact I can tell my hon. friend that the price of fish has gone up for this season by reason of the very fact that we have strict regulations which will maintain the best quality possible in our export fish. Recently it was advertised that owing to these regulations there had been an increase in the price from 30 cents per fish in 1932 to 40 cents in 1933. My hon. friend states that these regulations have been asked for by a limited number of canners who want to control the market. The information we have is that the companies who desire to have the regulations maintained put up ninety-three per cent of the pack. These companies own forty-two out of forty-four canneries which were operated last year. There are seventeen in number, and thirteen of these companies operate only one cannery each. It is obvious therefore that nearly all the small canners as well as the large canners favour the regulations. It is not a matter of only a few canners, but over ninety per cent of the canners are in favour of it.
No.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
And they contend that the price of fish is going up on account of these very regulations. I have here a statement prepared by an expert of my department and I wish to give it in full:
It is an acknowledged fact that following the development of sharp competition amongst the canneries in British Columbia the quality of the pack went down. This was due to the fish
LMr. Duranleau.]
being too long after being caught before they were canned. A prominent reason for this was the distance that fish was frequently carried. The result of this, together with growing competition from the orient and United States, was that British Columbia fish were losing their position on most important markets.
What is the date of that?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
April 24, 1933. I
asked for it because I think it is well that it should be placed before the committee.
To overcome this situation, inspection of the canned product was started last year.
My hon. friend referred to that regulation. He opposed it bitterly last year and now he admits that it was successful in its operation.

After being five times
amended.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
Yes, but only in
administrative details. It is always found necessary in important regulations of the sort to have minor amendments made. A few months' experience shows that slight amendments are necessary, but this regulation is to-day working in the interests of the fishermen.
Owing to the fact that there are five species of salmon, that the same species differs in quality in different areas and differs in the same area in different years, an adequate classification for inspection of canned salmon has so far been found in any country to be impracticable. Canada has gone further than any other country has yet been able to go, though its inspection is a minimum. It provides merely that fish that are fresh, firm, well packed and in good merchantable condition shall be entitled to a certificate, while all that are fit for human consumption but fall below these requirements shall be definitely marked "second quality." and those below second quality shall be confiscated.
Just when a fish ceases to be fresh and firm is a matter on which there is bound to be difference of opinion amongst experts, but there can be no doubt that fish begin to get soft practically from the time they are dead and that this process goes on slowly or rapidly, depending on conditions. This is recognized in the fish packing world. In Scotland, for instance, where herring is the main factor in the industry and where it is put up in barrels, it is required that fish to be entitled to the brand, must be placed in the barrels within twenty-four hours after being caught.
The board of inspection both before and since its appointment, strongly urged the importance of fish reaching the canneries promptly after being caught.
In no competing country are fish carried a greater distance than the amended regulation allows. As a usual thing the distance is very much less.
It is only when the quality of the pack as a whole is good enough that adequate prices can be obtained, and the fishermen consequently paid the best possible prices.

Supply-Fisheries

It makes very little difference to me whether the minister expresses his own views or reads something from an expert, it all comes from the lost and found department anyway. He quotes the cannery men, and states that they represent ninety per cent, but how is that ninety per cent made up? The statement reads that it was subsequently strongly recommended to the department on behalf of those who put up over ninety per cent of the canned product. Yes, but the three big canning companies claim that they put up over ninety per cent of the product. I have no evidence that they do, but that is their claim.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
There are seventeen
companies.

The next suggestion made is that they are going to ask for a sworn statement. The life of a cannery man is hard enough; he is losing lots of money and he should not be damned for the next world by being asked to take such an oath. He should not be asked to swear before God that the salmon was landed at such a time when in fact he did not see it landed. It may have been landed at another one of his canneries a hundred miles away. The minister refers to Scotland. Do they can salmon in Scotland to the extent they do in British Columbia? He speaks about herring in barrels, but are salmon packed in barrels? He tells us that the fishermen are going to get better prices for their salmon this year. Surely in vain the net is spread in the sight of any bird. These fishermen are not fools and they are not going to be caught by an argument as specious as that. I have the papers to prove my point, but I cannot lay my hand upon them at the moment. I have half a dozen articles taken from local papers, some of them quoting the chief supervisor of fisheries of British Columbia. He is an expert, and he states that the sockeye was practically sold out and it was inevitable that the price would rise. They are asking us to believe that the passing of this order in council was responsible. This order in council could not possibly take effect for months and months, in fact they do not even know how to enforce it, yet they ask us to believe that it was because of this that the price immediately shot up. My opinion is that this rise in price was because of the low pack in the past two years, coupled with the increasing demand in one or two countries. When the demand goes up, of course the price goes up. It would be much better from a political point of view for the government to
claim that this rise in price was because of their stabilization measure. I have never hesitated to give the government credit for taking that action; I only wish they had gone a little further and included lumber. They did a good thing and perhaps it has stimulated the price so that it begins at 40 cents. After all, 40 cents is not such a spectacular price. We think of some British Columbia cannery men giving the fishermen 40 cents out of the generosity of their hearts, but it must be remembered the last year they were paying United States fishermen 40 and 45 cents. Quantities of salmon were brought in from the States and that price was paid in American currency. It is not such a great potlach to the fishermen to start the price at 30 cents. If the minister was sincere in talking about quality, why does he not give the regulations passed last year the year of trial asked for? The minister says that these regulations were amended in a few details, but I contend that they were amended in many substantial details. They were five and a half times as long as they had been previously. Will they show their sincerity by amending this regulation, and instead of having it read " landed at the cannery twenty-four hours after being caught," make it read " canned thirty-six hours after being caught"? I challenge the minister to consider this matter from that point of view.

I have another tfiatter I would like to bring to the attention of the minister in connection with Japanese fishing licences. I understand that in 1923 a reduction of 40 per cent was made in these licences and when the matter was considered by the committee in 1924 it was decided that no reduction would be made that year. It was later recommended by the committee that there would be a further reduction of 15 per cent for the season of 1925 and in the following year it was recommended that beginning with 1927 there would be a yearly reduction of 10 per cent, based on the number in force in 1926. As the matter had got into the courts it was decided that no reduction would be made until the courts had rendered a decision. The situation is becoming very serious. The total licences issued in the province last year were as follows:
Whites	 6,486
Japanese	 2,143
Indians	 2,800
The situation is much more serious, however, on the Fraser river where the proportion of Japanese is much larger. In that district the licences issued to whites number 852 as against 586 issued to Japanese. These were
Supply-Fisheries

the figures for 1932 as given by the department. Because of the application made to the courts, I believe the yearly 10 per cent reduction was held up pending decision. As I understand it, since the passing of the statute of Westminster, Canada can now deal exclusively with such matters as the granting of licences. Some years ago certain associations protested against the cut, but at a meeting which I attended in New Westminster it was stated that these protests had been made under a misapprehension. Last year the association went on record as unanimously favouring the reduction in the number of licences issued' to Japanese. In previous years the department has taken the attitude that these Japanese were working on the sea, and that if they were taken away from fishing it would mean just that many more on the land, but the fact is that they are going on the land in greater numbers than ever The increase in population by birth is very rapid. Last year in the schools there was a 38 per cent increase in population of Japanese as against five per cent of whites. The question was raised in the British Columbia legislature last year and the Hon. Mr. Maitland made this statement:
Hundreds of false birth certificates have been issued in British Columbia, particularly in the case of orientals. Hon. It. L. Maitland, minister without portfolio, said in the legislature Monday, on moving second reading o-f a bill which would "tighten up" restrictions.
Under the statutes at present a citizen may take out a deferred certificate, he explained. "Japanese have been going back as long as twenty-five years ago in claiming birth in the province. As a consequence, many Japanese who were not born in British Columbia at all not only get certain fishing rights but passport privileges as British subjects."
Last year I brought up the matter-it does not touch the minister's department-regarding immigration and I then stated to the Minister of Immigration I believed more than fifty per cent of the Japanese in British Columbia were in that province illegally. I have before me the report of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police for the year ended September 30, 1932, in which I find a very serious statement and one that practically confirms what I said in the house at that time. This has a bearing on my appeal to the minister regarding the Japanese and fishing licences. On page 50 of this report I find the following statement by Superintendent Wood:
With regard to the Department of Immigration and Colonization, Superintendent Wood says:
"The investigation regarding the infractions of immigration and other acts of Japanese in British Columbia is still being carried on vigorously, and I am of the opinion that the situation is more serious than we previously imagined."
[Mr. Reid.)
This is the superintendent who is saying that it is more serious.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: And prosecutions of those guilty of fraud were carried out.

That is very true, but I am now coming to the fishery licences. Superintendent Wood says:
Recently the investigation has disclosed that numerous naturalization certificates are held by persons other than their owners in the Skeena river area. The number so held is estimated to be over 150, and one source of information places the number as high as 400.
This is the official report.
These certificates are being used to illegally obtain fishing licences.
That is a very serious statement and it should be taken due cognizance of. I am speaking particularly however of conditions in the Fraser river. I understand a movement was initiated by the British Columbia Protective Association asking the minister to continue the cut of ten per cent in licences until the Japanese were eliminated, as had been proposed a few years previously. The Japanese, I might say, are becoming arrogant on the Fraser river. The information is also given to me that they now dominate certain branches of the fishing industry on the lower mainland of British Columbia. I have before me a letter from a dealer in codfish in Vancouver who states, with regard to codfishing:
At present it is dominated and controlled by the Japanese. In Vancouver all the codfish brought in by any nationality is sold through M. Myamoto, a Japanese.
If, for instance, you went codfishing and brought your catch into Vancouver you would have to dispose of it through M. Myamoto.
He tells me in this letter that if I want any further information regarding the matter, he will be glad to give it. We have among our own nationals men who control certain industries, but the situation is more serious when you have a Japanese controlling a business in our own country because all his dealings are directed with more benefit to his race than to the white people of Canada. As I have stated the Japanese are becoming very arrogant on the Fraser river, and last fall I had drawn to my attention a case where they threatened bodily harm because a white man dared to be around one of the little islands in the mouth of the Fraser river endeavouring to catch some fish with a line. Another case occurred in the same year up north where a Japanese boat ran through a white man's boat and the two white men would have been drowned had they not been picked up by another fishing boat which happened to be near by. The Japanese use

people of their own race all the time. Their trucks take care of their own stores and practically all their business centres around the Japanese. Last fall, when the market in Japan was low, the Japanese saw to it that only Japanese on the Pacific coast received any consideration in regard to the sale of salted or smoked fish that was destined for Japan.
I am appealing to the minister regarding this; I am asking him on behalf of the Fraser river fishermen, who are unanimously in favour of the cut being continued, that he recommence the reduction of licences in so far as the Japanese are concerned. Our own people should be better looked after and encouraged. The argument formerly used that if you chased the Japanese off the rivers and the ocean, they would go on to the land, no longer holds good, because they are on the land anyway and in greater numbers than before, even though there are just as many Japanese fishermen. In my constituency there is one school of fourteen rooms. Eleven of them are wholly Japanese; one only is white and the others are half Japanese and half white. In a school not far from where I live, last year I saw eleven boys at play, nine of whom were Japanese and two white. That shows the extent of the growth in population of the Japanese on the land in British Columbia. The fishermen are now protesting and on their behalf I am asking the minister to consider recommencing the cut in the licences of the Japanese and favouring our own people.
Progress reported.
